" CAPITAL " CHAT.
Madame Patti, who has just arrived in New York, was the only passenger on the City of Paris who did not become a victim to sea sickness.

WHAT animal always plays a leaning part in life? A blind man's dog. key said that even the most honest blacksmith will' sometimes pick a Jock. THE grave-digger's advice to the stock-specs- latoseeeklimaya be ready for the last call. " Time rainest in this bosom," as the lover said when a basin of water was thrown over him by the lady he was serenading. A GENTLEMAN who has been struck by a lady's beauty has determined to follow the injunction and "kiss the rod that smote him. Aim you asleep, Susey?" "Why do you alik tne such a question, ma ? "Because it's time to take your medicine ?" "Then I'm &glee?, ma." Baowir says it is a wonder there is any truthful- ness in world when mankind begins life by lying in the cradle: WHEN would you expect a man to suffer from a stitch in his side? When he is hemmed in by a crowd. Sweer CONCLUSION.—" So far ao good," as 'the boy said when he had finished the hrst pot of his mother's jam. "WHAT possesses you, my dear, who have such 'an excellent husband, to make him angry so often ?" " Because he always brings use a present to make peace again." ASSESSOR (to a . fartner)--e"This land here seems to be yery fertile." Farmer—" Yes, very. Even when the crops fail the taxesgrow right along from year to year." " You are growling bald, Envy," said Jones to his friend Brown, whom he basi not seen for severe-1 years. "I am bald," replied Brown; "but I ant not growing any snore." "JOHN," said a eigid -disciplinarian to his son, "have you kept that diary.l gave you on your last birthday!" "Yes, father. I put it in the bottom of my trunk, and have kept it there ever since, SD that nobody could get it away from me." "SARAH JANE; what :book is that you're reading so steadily all the time ?" "It's a novel, by Dumas, the elder?' Don't tell me! Dumas the elder? What church could he be elder in and write novels, I should like to know ?" "DON'T you suppose," said a member of the police force, "that a policeman knows &rogue when he sees him ?" "No doubt," was the reply; "but the trouble is that he -does not seize a rogue when he knows him." LAME'S sonnet, entitled "The Gipsy's Malison," was returned to him by the editors of the maga- zines. In a letter to a friend he told him of the failure, and added humorously, "D—the ace; I'll write for antiquity." "How do you eke May? I've been trying to catch up with you for half an hour." "Howt'did you know it was I?" "Oh ! I knew you just as soon as I set eyes en that bonnet. I've known it as long as I can remember." It is such remarks as these that fill the female heart with bitterness. AMCSING AND CHEAP.—" Why do you always invite Pitancharcl to your house ?" "He is an old friend." " 'noes -no reason. He is horribly ugly, and he gives Ere the nightmare." `• Yes ; but be amuses the children re) much, and it's much cheaper than a magic lantern !" A rnovesson, in explaining to a clays of young ladies the theory according to which the body is entirely renewed every seven years, said, "Thus, Miss 8., in seven years you will in reality be no longer Miss B." ".I really hope I shan't," de- murely responded the girl, casting down her eyes. A WESTEZN man sent in to the editor of a local paper an item to the effect that his fiftieth wedding anniversary would be observed on a certain day. To his disgust, when the announcement appeared, it was found that the printer had left out the weed "anniversary." MR SAMPLESON iS a very irascible man, and is in the habit of punishing his boys very severely. ; Not long since he observed that one of his sons needed a new pair of trousers. He scolded the boy for wearing outhis clothes so fast. "Pa, no trousers can last any time the way you hits," re- plied the son, reproachfully. THERE was a heated discussion in an hotel the other night. " I tell y3u, sir," said one of the disputants, "there is no law made but what the people can change." "Yes, there is," said a new- comer, "there is one law that no man—no people can ohange." "What is that ?" "A mother-in- law." A MAN out West, Who married a widow, has in- vented a device to cure her of eternally praising her former husband. Whenever she begins to descant on his noble qualities, this ingenious No. 2 merely says, "Poor, .dear man! How I wish he hadn't died !" and the lady immediately thinks of something else to talk about. AN innocent lad -one evening went up to the drawing-room on the bell being rung. When he returned to the kitchen he laughed immoderately. Sawed the servants asking the cause of his mirth, he cried, "What do you think? There are sixteen of them who could not snuff the candles, and were obliged to send for me tredo it." The marriage of Miss Jane Cobden with Mr. T. Fisher Unwin, will, I hear, take place on the 2nd prox., at the Parish, Church of Heyshott, Sussex, the place where Richard Cobden was born, and near where he is buried. Mr. T. B. Potter, :MX., will give the bride away.

A great deal has been said of the magnificence of the house in Prince's-gate which the late Mr. F. P. Leyland purchased from Lord Somers. One pecu- liarity of it, however, has escaped notice, and that is the subterranean study, which was fitted up with every luxury for the use of the owner.

All the arrangements for the Royal wedding we.re made before the Duke of Clarence wus attacked by influenza, and the carrying out ot these de- pended, of course, upon the recovery made by Ins Royal Highness. The wedding was to take place in St. George's Chapel, at Windsor, on Saturday, the 27th of Februaiy, at a quarter to one.

Mr. Chaplin, being released front attendance :at Osborne, is off to the Sleaford Division to keep those agricultural labourers sweet, and to persuade them that notwithstanding Lord Salisbury's remarks about circuses being more fit for villages than councils, the Minister of Agriculture will be their friend, notithe conveners of Memorial Hall Confer- ewes.
CODI

Madame Melba and some members of a provincial opera company have taken part (according to the "Echo du Nord ") in a representation of " Taust," before the employees of a local brewer in the 1 siiburlys of Lille, the opera ' being given in the branding abed on a stage constructed on barrels. In tbiacountry beer supports the peerage, in F ranee • the opera. The French are always artistic.

Jam informed that Mrs. Osborne's whereabouts are very well known, and that only considerations' of 'humanity stand between her and arrest. It is, her intention, as soon as her present trouble is over to return to England and take her trial. She is at a piece somewhat south of Madrid,and it is believed that by arrangement a detective officer is staying in the immediate neighbourhood. This will account for the delay which has taken place in the execu- Count the warrant.

The bunday School Union is organising alrip to Rome for Sunday School teachers and those inte- rested in Sunday Schools. The party will leave London about the 22nd of February and return home ~n the sth March. The proposed route will be from London to Paris via Newhaven and )Dieppe, and thence by the Mont Cenis runnel and Turin to Rome, returning via Venice and Milan, through the St. Gothard Tunnel to Lucerne, thence by may of Paris to London.

As was to be expected, the London record from influenza last week shows a marked increase. The total-95---exceeds by 22 the aggregate of the three vreceding weeks. A remarkable feature a the statistics is the comparative immunity of young people from fatal results. Eight only of those who died were under the age of five; and of those be- tween the ages of five and 20 but two succumbed. The heaviest record is of persons betweenthe ages Of 60 and 80, of whom 39 died.

Mr. Waddy, M.P., Q.C., is in a very precarious state of health. What with his: legal duties and the political calls upon his time, be has for some time been overworking and neglecting to take proper rest. Sometimes for days together this only sleep was snatched in the train, when travelling to London. The result was a serious attack of rheumatism, which was got rid of by timely treat- ment, but rheumatism was only a symptom of more deeply-seated trouble. He has now been obliged to cease all work, and go to the Riviera for a complete rest and change of scene.

Bishop Philpott, who has died in the home of his retirement at Cambridge, was without excep- tion the most popular man in his crowded diocese. Everywhere when his name was uttered admiration of his character was expressed, and rare indeed was a carping criticism or unkind comment heard. As ' ke was known in hie diocese during the later years of his life, the Bishop was wofully thin and em- aciated. Ills gaunt, haggard figure, plodding patiently to and fro in the streets of any of the towns of Worcestershire, was sure of recognition as much for this peculiarity as because of the devotion of his flock to the study of clerical personnel.

Dr. yhilpott's devotion to his blind wife was as touching as any incident of the kind ever recorded It was the aim of his life to diminish by every gentle office and tender consideration the great burden of her infirmity. Occasionally she would appear in public at prize-givings or village fetes;' and then it was pathetic to see the aged Bishop leading her forward on the platform, placing the prizes in her hand, and guiding that hand in the direction of the winner, for whom she always had a smile and a word of encouragement.

In a letter to the Marquis of Salisbury Mr Henry I Varley calls attention to a pretty state of things existing in the British island of Singapore. In the year 1890 no fewer than 160,000 Chinese coolies were imported into the island. They are shipped from various Chinese ports by agents on more or less false pretences. They sign contracts which practically give these agents the command of their wages. When they arrive at Singapore they are herded in huge sbede,and then let out by the agent, who contracts to supply coolie labor at various places throughout the Eastern Archipelago. Unless, in short, Mr. Varley has discovered a mare's nest, Singapore is the headquarters of a gigantic slave traffic, carried on under the protection of the British flag, and admitted by "a prominent Government official to be this and nothing better. The state- ments at least call for further investigation.

A new chemical industry has arisen, that of colouring natural cut flowers. A Paris Correspon- dent writes: For some time the florists have been selling at fancy prices all kinds of flowers, which were supposed to be the roc's eggs of hortieultu- lists, such as sky blue orchids, pink. narcissuses, green and violet roses, and ultramarine chrysan- themums. It now appears that the flowers were simply dyed by a new process, which MM. Charles Girard and Pabst have revealed. The colouring matters are dissolved in variable quantities,accord- ' ing to the depth of the hues that are to be obtained, in filtered water, in which, to hasten the solution f he co matter, a few drops of alcohol have of thepoured. The stalk ends of the flower are then placed in the dye, and the fluid by capillary attrac- tion is drawn up into the flower. The dye, how- ever, .only colours freshly-cut flowers, nor will watering the roots of a plant with the colouring matter produce the effect.

:HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 16, 1892. CROSS CENTRAL AMERICA.,

I was so near; but I pushed on, and here I am in I Massachusetts, and likely to begin work in the largest wire mill in the world, so it is said. Thou- sands of miles are now between me and my loved ones. When we shall meet again I don't know. Fate seems hard with me ; perhaps I deserve it all; I don't know. Be it as it may,l am getting weary of it, and I sometimes feel as if I should like to lay it all down. I long with a longing past all descrip- tion, for an abiding place with those I love. Shall I ever find it on earth ? I know not. _ _ _

B U. WiIITLIAIL. Although I place the above heading to this letter, I want my good friends in Warrington to krow that I am writing in a nice warm room, seated at a win- dow through which I can look over the telds of a sweet New English village. I can also see the, snow disappeanneneath the pressure of a sharp dry frost. 111 this is somewhat new tome I hope' it will be beneficial to my health, as this is not all I could desire. Where did my readers and Ilast part company / Somewhere near Champerico, on the Mexican coast I think. If they look on tlie map of the American continent, they will Cid Puget Sound running out between that and British Columbia. Or, just look around Cape Flattery for Saohomish. On the tanks of this river with an old Indian name I spent a couple of days, as in a previous letter de- scribed. From there let the reader beat his way by Portland through the State of Waslington, on through Oregon, and enter California at Ashland. From thence by Mount Shasta he is brought on the Switch-back track across the Siskiyons en to Sacra- mento, and so onto San Francisco. After a couple of days spent with my family, again on the move. This time
Greendale, Worcester, Mass., December 17, 1891.

ACROSS THE PA.crirc OCEAN' or as it used to be called in the old Sparish galleon days, the Spanish main. Keeping Lower Califor- nia well in view, we pass on, under a burning sun, and over a sea like a sheet of glass. Oh, but is'nt it splendid! I never felt so much before the want of a facile pen, and the power to give out again, what was passing before my eyes. The ship calls at the Mexican ports, to take in cargo and to dis- charge, staying as required, one, two, and three 'days. Opportunity is given to passengers to land. I We cannot avail ourselves of this opportunity after we leave Acapuleo, as a .charge of two dols. per head is made as a sort of 13011 tay At Acapuleo we went on shore and spent the day, and far into the night. 1 cannot tell what the heat was, but it was something to remember. Everybody seemed to be just able to move about. Clothing, being a super- fluity, was cast aside. Men and women en every hand were swinging in their hammocks, all intent on one thing,smoking theincigars, emptying cocoa- nuts of their sweet milk, eating bananas, and once in a while a pine apple. These little matters, with a gossip indifferently well carried on with the natives, helped the day along. To walk out amongst the vegetation was rather hazardous, with prickly bushes of a sort that made one think Dame Nature had made special efforts to provide against the incursions of man. It is very nice to look at the cactus, but to feel it suddenly in close proximity with one's understandings> apt to raise all the old Adam we mortals carry about with us. Further inland we were told were plenty of monkeys and parrots, but snakes and lizards under foot, and our hot friend, the sun, above, us warned us to get near the shore again. When evening came, we saw, what we werelassured west° be seen every evening— the plaza, a beautiful square filled with flowering magnolias and tall cocoanut trees, laid out with long tables and large square tables for the evening's gamble. Yes, this is THE PARA.DISE tOF THE GAMBLER. Every one, old, and young, rich and poor, gambles and drinks muscat. Lamps hung all around make the scene picturesque. A party of Mexican bull-fighters had come down, intending to sail with us. I think these fellows have a notion they are the aristocrats of the land. In their gold-brai(led jackets they strut about like American millionaires, with their tall sombreros, which, I am told cost all the way up to 50 and 500 dollars; they look perfect pictures of conceit. When tired of all this we take boat and go sailing across the bay to our ship. Here we find all hard at work ; that has lost all its interest for us. Before.turning in,we spend an hour watching the sharks. The water is literally alive with them. Big monsters they are. Every moment a great head is shoved out of the water, causing one to shudder at what the possible result would be of an accidental fall over should come to any of us. Well, all this, like other things, comes to an end, and we weigh anchor, leaving Mexico and the shores of the United States of British Columbia be- hind us. Before leaving this part of my narrative, I must say, from all I could learn, that IT IS A VERY RICH COUNTRY, a country whose people simply detest America and all belonging to her, a country that stands waiting for English capital. Had Mexico had Englishmen within her borders, instead of France forcing a Maximilian upon her, to-day would h ave seen a very different state of things. England would have had a flourishing trade here. The country is rich in ores, rich in vegetation, with a soil that needs little persuasion to give forth in abundance. A know- ledge of Spanish would be needed. This can begot hold of with little trouble. To get hold of the Mexican tongue would entail great labour, and this is not necessary.
NOW FOR PANAMA.

Little did I think years ago when reading o Lessep'a work that I should travel over it, and see it in all its gigantic failings. A car line crosses the Isthmus, carrying 'cargo and passengers to a ship that awaits at Aspinwall. It takes about three hours to cross: a right and fit name for this coun- try would be that of the dismal swamp. One con- tinued pestilential, malaria-breathing atmosphere hangs around and clings to us. It is scarcely pos- sible to imagine how human beings can possible live here. From every thatch-roofed cabin steam rises. On every sloop, naked urchins sit, or listlessly look around. The native population is black, with the strange peculiarity that the women folk dress in a plentiful supply of white starched skirts. Washing days must be frequent, as rain cad mud seem to be as plentiful as banana trees, of which there were no end. What a sight is this Lesseps failure! All along the car track are corrugated roofed houses built for the labourers. livery few miles are centres from which the works were con- ducted. These centres are now deserted; all life is gone, but not the machinery. No, this is left to rot, and rust away. Great steam dredges, by the score, tip waggons by the thousands. I counted in one long row over twenty locomotivea,and of these rows there seemed to be scores. There had been some painting going on, with the view, I suppose, of preserving this costly machinery. I cannot fancy what this is for. To remove this machinery would cost as much as it is worth, and I cannot fancy the work ever going on again. White men could not work here ; they could but boss, and at this died off quick. It is said here that for every sleeper laid in the track upon which we ride, a labourer sleeps beneath it. I can quite believe it. I, like the rest of my fellow travellers, was mighty glad to reach Aspinwall, where we found B.S. city of Para waiting for us, and ready to steam out at once. It must be understood-that it is always the previous ship's cargo that is shipped so as not to keep passengers on these shores a minute longer i than s possible. Before leaving these malarial shores, I want to describe in a few words a sight I think the most interesting I ever saw. It occurred while crossing the Pacific. Havingretired early one evening to my bunk, I was aroused by some one calling out, " Whitham," or, if I must be quite trsthful, " Professor,come on deck and tell us what this is." Well, it was a sight not to forget. On each side, or under each bow, were ranged in line, shoulder to shoulder, at least A DOZEN ELECTRIC The Jacks told us they were porpoises. I scarcely thought so, but there they were, covered with clouds of electricity, which seemed to strip off each fish, or animal as it tired and retired, from the ranks. As each one fell out, another came in out of the darkness, and took orderly rank. It was dark each evening,and the sight of these fish going with the ship as if yoked to her, and pulling her along, formed one of the most wonderful and beautiful sights it was ever my privilege to behold. Turtles , in abundance are seen in these latitudes lazily sail- ing along like logs of wood, but these we must pass over and hasten on to the ship. Anchor weighed again, off we Start for New York. We these given Cape Horn the go by, and so escaped her storms, but we are now in the IN orth Atlantic, and we are anxious as to how we shall fare. The Atlantic has a bad reputation: everyone looks for storms, especi- ally at this time of the year. If the first few days pass all right, we are still kept nervous by the as- surance that we shall certainly have a blow off Cape Hatteras. Well, we pass the Gulf of Mexico, we pass the stormy Cape, nay we pass Sandy Hook, and quietly gliding into dock at New York, we knew we had CHEATED ALL THE STOEDIS and proved the prophets false ones. Yes,the whole voyage of four weeks had been done without even a lift of the vessel, and here I was on terra firma, having from the commencement sailed almost around the immense American continent, how many thousands of miles I don't know. Well, the time paused pretty well. I made great friends with the dozen Jack tars who were returning to their homes from the Behring seas. I ought to know something of the Fisheries Question, for I have heard it argued often enough. I felt, when at New 'fork, that I should like to run over and sae you all,

THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," &c., &c.
CHAPTER V. IN THE LADY'S WALK.
,mrtother person was also watching the beautiful sunset, without, however, perceiving anything of an

ideal nature in it. There was a walk at the bottom of the hall garden, a walk shadowed and overhung with trees; and this formed the favourite promenade of Madam. To this place she resorted when she wished to be alone, and here she paced to and fro in the fading light, in a strangely noiseless, stealthy fashion, and very rapidly withal. Set and hard was her face, and a restless glitter

shone in her eyes. Ever and anon she paused, and threw an im- patient glance in the direction of the house. From the open windows of her husband's sanctum—the room he devoted to the entertainment of his friends and boon companions—floated out on the air sounds 'of noisy laughter and unbridled mirth. Squire Breamish had been on his company manners during the visit of the Callerleys ; and now, the restraint of their presence removed, felt a sudden necessity for relaxation. He was there- fore haviag his usual after-dinner carouse, of which he had been hitherto defrauded, and with no more 'fitting companions than his gamekeeper and head fitableman.

" With hound and horn, of a misty morn, A hunting down the glen, Rode lithe young Jack, with his trusty pack, With a curse to all lie-a-bed men." As the rollicking voices, trolling ,out an old hunting ditty, reached Madam's ears, a sudden paroxysm of rage seized upon her, aed shook her from head to foot. She stamped her shoe upon the gravelled path in a very ecstasy of passion. It was seldom that she permitted her temper to break loose, because her will was sufficiently strong to do battle with it; but whenever it did manage to bear down all restraint, it was indeed overpower- ing, and almost sublime. During these intervals Madam rose to the grandeur of a Medea or a Clytemnestra. "Fool, fool ! "she now exclaimed, in self-derision, throwing her hands into the air with an intensely tragic, because an intensely hopeless, gesture, "what unlucky star ruled my destiny, that this decaying estate and degraded name should be my share of this world's goods? To be gifted with brains and with wit; a moderate share of good looks; blue blood in one's veins, and, . . ay, and passion too—and to do no better than that ! ' . . . Here she cast another contemptuous kir& in the direction of the open windows. "Dorothy Breamish, you have indeed played your cards badly ! " She walked to and fro in silence for a while, and then her chagrin burst into words again. "And a baby-faced girl to carry off the prize I would once have perilled my soul to gain. A girl who is little better than a fashionable doll, and knows neither how to hate, nor to love a man. Ah, Lancelot, you are too true a Callerley to be long content with such a child wife as that. Your heart is too much like unto mine—ever husgry, restless, dissatisfied ! "Why did you not love me, Lancelot Callerley? I thought that I had got over my passion for you, and was half-satisfied to dream, instead of to love. It is an ill hour that has brought us together again, unless—unless, nay I must not finish that sentence. We are of the same proud, implacable, passionate nature. Yes, and for that reason we should have understeed each other more completely than could any other of alien blood! Had you but loved me, I could have become a good woman, ay, even a sweet one, for your dear sake. Nothing in the world would have troubled me, so that I had possessed your affections. Even the shadow that hangs over our house." Here she stopped suddenly, and shivered, as with cold. At that moment the sound of boyish laughter mingled with the voices of the revellers, and then little Lance appeared at one of the windows blowing, or attempting to blow, an old hunting horn which he had picked up from the table. "That's right, lad," roared the Squire, in a thick, husky voice, "Copy thy dad, and thou% be an ornament to the name of Breamish By Diana but the youngster bids fair to follow in my foot- steps in the matter of sport, though Madam does hold that he features the Callerleys". "Heaven forbid he copy you in anything ; " murmured Mrs. Breamish, and then she called the lad to her in a clear peremptory voice, which did not admit of question. Whistling to the old hound to accompany him, the boy clambered out over the window-sill; sing- ing as he did so : " With hound and horn of a misty morn," and imitating the various sounds of a foxyhunt with great skill and spirit. "Lance, my darling, I do wish you would not be so fond of everying appertaining to the stables! I want you to be a gentleman, and a Callerley, not a mere fox-hunting squire." "Dad is a fox-hunting Squire, I suppose, mother, and you look down upon him for it But even cousin Lancelot said that hunting was fine sport for Englishmen, and cousin Lancelot is perfect, you know! Mother, lam fond of poor old Dad, and don't want to be any different to him, except that I will not get drunk ; because you see a man looks such a fool when he is in liqour, and I never like being laughed at! And when lam old enough, I shall have a pretty little wife just like Lady Callerley, and if she chooses to laugh at me it won't matter so much, because she is sweet and good- natured." What? you too, my son ?".thought Madam, with a bitter spasm. "Do you not love me sufficiently to wish to be the sort of son I should be proud of, Lance?" she said, with wistful sadness, "has your mother no influence upon you ? " Lance cast down his eyes, and played with the riding whip he carried. " I did not mean that, mother," he replied in a confused manner. "You do not seem to care sometimes, and I—l did not know you wanted me to love you so much !" To his great surprise this mother answered this by snatching him to her, and kissing him with passionate vehemence, over and over again. What have I left to love, if my own refuses to love me?" she exclaimed, with fierce emotion. "Oh, Lance, Lance, if you did but know how my heart aches sometimes ! ' She burst into violent weeping, and Lance, who had never before seen her so moved, was half afraid, half pitiful. " Don't, manimy dear, don't cry like that, and /1l love you better than anyone except Uncle Jack, I will indeed !" He tried to get his little arms around her, but her softened mood, sudden and brief, like most of her emotions, was passing, and she pushed him away in an impatient way. "Go " she cried quickly, "go back to your father, and his—his shameful company ! lam not well, and you trouble me." With wondering, wistful looks, the boy instantly obeyed, and in her capricious mood, she resented his obedience. "He is glad to go. Glad to leave the mother who can neither win his love nor amuse him ! What is there in me, that prevents my gaining the affection of any human being? Am I a monster, created by an unjust God, simply to be abhorred, and to excite hatred in the place of affection ? " With morbid persistence, she dwelt upon this point, and wept over it with self pity, though she was not generally given to tears. But that clay. ,envy, natred, and Malice had entered deeply into her soul, and completely distorted her mental After a while, however, she grew calmer, and when the pointe of light began to twinkle out of the dusky sky, the passionate rebellious mood had passed. "Poor Lance! I wish I had been softer, and kinder to him:! There is some tenderness for me latent in the lad, after all, if I only knew how to bring it to the ourface. But I have no gift of charming, no winning ways. That girl to-day—she charmed without the slightest effort. Even Harry, dull, insensible Barry, was movedto enthusiasm by her pretty looks and words. And yet I try so hard sometimes, so very, very hard. Study to make my voice soft, and my smiles sweet. What is it that is lacking, without which all my care is of no avail! "Poor little Lance 1 Well, there is something left me to be thankful for after all. Strange ! that the very admixture of blood from a dull sire should be a source of satisfaction and—and of safety. There is coMpensation in that thought, even for what I have suffered. Yes, Lancelot is right there. He ought to be the last of the Callerleys. It was weak inexcusably weak in him to marry. As for me, J. must smile on, while poverty, ruin, maybe disgrace, come marching upon us. A woman is irretrievably lost if the links her fate with that

NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Life's Handicap: being stories of mine own peo- ple " is the title of the latest work of fiction by Mr. Itudyard Kipling. It is published by Messrs. Mac- millan and Company, and, like the previous volume of stories by this extraordinary writer, it is likely to have a large sale. The leading tale, "The in- carnation of Chrishna Mulvaney" is told with wonderful power and humour. It reveals an inti- mate acquaintance with the British soldier,as is the case with most of the stories relating to life in India. The author has a genius for picturesque ' description. Not that there is any elaborate word- painting. On the contrary, he depicts a scene or describes a character in a few short vigorous sen- tencea which take the reader to the heart of the matter. Ile has a style which is peculiarly his own, both of plot and narrative. There is evidence of condensation in every page, and the result is that every page is racy. There is not one of these stories which can be said to be like its fellow, and they are all excellent We can strongly recommend "Life's Handicap" to all who are on the look-out for something vigorous and original. "John Inglesant," also published by Messrs. Macmil- lan and Co., is a work, too, in the region of romance, nf a character altogether different from the book just noticed. The writer, Mr. J. 11. Shorthouse, is scholarly and philosophical, with a keen eye to the spiritual element in character. In this story he gives a vivid picture of life in the 17th century, and particularly in relation to the civil war which ended in the execution

of Charles I. The hero, John Inglesant, becomes a ser- vant of Charles, and is entrusted at various times with important missions,in one of which he is placed in such a peculiar position that he must either injure the king or be untrue to himself. He decides on the latter course, declaring that certain letters are forged, 'which are really in the handwriting of the king. All the interest of the novel as to this incident is in preserving the res- pect of the reader fora man who can still be called high- minded, even when he is, misguidedly, doing a wrong thing. The relation in which Inglesant stands, midway in training and opinion between the English and the Romish Church, enables the author to develope some singular features of character, and at the same time enunciate his own views, as a scholar and a thinker. There is an ,elernent of mysticism in the novel, which becomes an added charm, especially as it affects the thoughts and deeds of "John Inglesant." Mr. Gladstone is amongst those who have a very high opinion of the story. Part 4 is to hand of the issue by the name firm of Green's" Short History of the English People." The period dealt with is that of the battle of Hastings. For frontispiece there is a map of the dominions of the Angevins ; and there are in addition a large number of admirably finished illustrations, which throw a special light upon the customs of the age under consideration. Printing, paper, and type are of the most superior kind. The parts are being published at Is. each. The " English Illustrated Magazine" is more than usually interesting with its illustrated papers on "Henry VIII. on the Stage," "A Tobacco Factory," "Wolf- Hunting in Russia," "The Sorting of Paupers,"" Fruit Ranching;" Sze. Messrs. F. Warne and Co., have issued a Is. 6d. work on " Electricity up to date, for light, power, and trac- tion." It is from the pen of Mr. J. B. Verity, and is cer- tainly the best manual on this subject that we have seen. So admirably and lucidly is the whole question dealt with, that a person of ordinary intelligence who has never before given thought to the subject can follow the author step by step, and understand the various methods by which electricity is brought into use for the service of man. In addition to accounts of the different modes of producing and applvin; electricity, details are given of the various public companies which are now In opera- tion. There is, too, a glossary of technical terms, besides a copious Index. " Barker's Facts and Figures "for 1892, published by William F. Warne and Company, is a capital shillings- worth. It, contains nearly 400 pages of well-prepared information on almost everything of moment to the inhabitants of this country, including two supplements one giving the results of the census returns, and the other furnishing particulars of the elections of 1885, and 1.886, and all the bye-elections since 1885. The "Century Magazine," for January has for a frontispiece a striking portrait of Charles Francis Gounod, and there is an article on " Gounod in Italy and Germany." The leading paper, profusely illus- trated. is on "The Jews in New York." Andrea Del Sarto is dealt with this month by Mr. W. J. Stillman, under the head of" Italian old Masters." Other power- fully illustrated papers are on " Custer's last battle ;" " The alligator bunters of Louisana ;" and "A battle in Crackerdom." There is a good supply of "In lighter vein ;" a completed story with the title of " Bentley's System," and a further instalment of" A story of west and east," by Rudyard Kipling and Wolcott Balestier. In the way 3f verse Mr. T. B. Aldrich has several con- tributions of a very high order. The leading paper in the current issue of "The Magaeine of Art "is on" John Russell, R.A., the prince of crayon portrait painters." The frontispiece is a beautiful photogravure of Russell's " Portrait of a lady," and there are several fine reproductions of his more notable pictures. Russell was of a religious turn of mind, and it is more suggestive than pleasant to find one of his notes running as follows : "Spending an evening at the Royal Academy, and obliged to leave because Of their filthy conversation." There is an article on "Artistic homes," by Mr. Reginald Blomfield, which is charmingly illustrated. Other illustrated papers are "Two winter exhibitions," " Book-edge decoration," " The Dulwich Gallery," and "Our illustrated note- book." The illustrations of "The Magazine of Art" are always geed, and in the current number they may be amid to reach their highest mark. " Caesell's Magazine" commences the year well. The frontispiece," betrothed," is very fine, and is from a drawing by Horwitz. The serial stories include "Out of the fashion," "You will love me yet," and " Had a notion." There are besides two complete stories, and amongst the miscellaneous illustrated papers we have " Treasure trove of Central Canada," " Christmas at Holly Bush Manor,"" Mount Mellic embroidery," "Chit chat on dress " and" The gatherer, a record of inven- tion, discovery, literature,and science." The" Quiver" maintains the high standard it has attained as an illustrated magazine for Sunday and gen- eral reading. In addition to three serial stories there are papers on" The gospel in the open air," "Sundays with the young," "Tools and workmen among the woods,"" Picotee," " Two ways of spending time," "Three conversions," " Short arrows,' &c.—" Little Folks "is all that could be desired with its stories and odds and ends in prose and verse, admirably written and cleaverly illustrated. The second 'part is published of "Don Quixote," as illustrated by Gustave Dor6. The work will be com- plete in 27 parts, at 3d. each, and will be unsurpassed at the price.—The fine art edition of "Robinson Crusoe "—and it is really fine—is completed with the issue of part 13 this month. We have also to hand from Messrs. Cassell and Co. the current parts of "The Dore Gallery," "Science for all," "Familiar wild flowers," "British battles," "Store- -house of general information," and " Figuier's: Popular Scientific Works." The subjects of the "Cabinet Portrait Gallery" for January are the Rev. Dr. Adeler, the Duchess of Edin- burgh, and Dr. Robson Roose. The photographs by Messrs. W. and D. Downey are "simply perfect," and there is in each case a brief and interesting biography, "The Ladies' Gazette of fashion," price ed., contains several coloured engravings and numerous other illustra- tions, and a needlework supplement. Amongst the matters dealt with we have" Gewns for evening wear ;" .4 Society and fashion,"" Pleasant and profitable occup- ations ; " A cosy window seat ; ' " A banquet under difficulties," " Home-made caps ;" "January in the garden, &c." We have also to hand a second edition of" Cornwall as a winter resort • " " A holiday trip round the Pem- broke Coast ; " and a brief description of Falmouth, Penzance, St. Ives, and the Scilly Isles,

CHAPTER. VI. SNOWED DP.

A storm of wind, or rather a succession of storms from the north-west, followed the beautiful sunset. Showers of snow, whirling and flying upon the air, but, save in sheltered places, scarcely covering the earth, came with these storms. Hoping against hope, and against their past expeaience, the country folk talked confidently of an early spring. "Grand weather for the ploughing. .A windy March and a showery April make a bonny May ! " , So they comforted themselves with proverbs, until the wind changed and, veering round to the east, caused great damage to the shipping on the coast, though, happily, there were no wrecks in the immediate vicinity of Callerley or Breamish. Lady Callerley chafed sadly under the enforced confinement to the house, and longed to be out of doors; the more so that Sir Lancelot had at last met with a suitable mount for her, a little mare of . .

, a bright bay colour, marked with a star on the fore- head, and Silvia was all impatient to try its paces. She could not conveniently gratify her fancy of calling it Hope, since it already possessed a name, Britomart, to which it answered in the sweetest imaginable way, following readily at the sound of its new mistress's voice, and rubbing its head against her shoulder. She was delighted with the acquisition, and would fain have gone out upon it through the storm, but on this point her husband was inexorable. She was not acclimatised yet, and this gale would certainly give her a cold, if noth- ing worse, did she venture out of doors. So she was obliged to content herself indoors, and kept flattening her pretty little nose against the window panes fifty times a day, to look if there were any sign of the'weather mending. Mending Little chance of that, at that time of the year, and in that backward part of the country. In place of menamg, the snow began to come down in earnest ; and the wind, playful at first, but wax- ing savage in its play, tossed it into drifts. In many sheltered valleys and denes, these same drifts grew, in less than a eouple of days, ten or twelve feet in depth. The turnpike road to the southward was blocked, and the mails altogether stopped for nigh upon a week. Lady Callerley felt this an added grievance, since she was troubled in mind about her scapegrace brother, and longed for letters. And,even when a way was at last opened and the mail bags were forwarded on horseback, no relief came to her. It was quite evident that both Lady Ormskirk and Teddy had already forgotten her. Day after day the frost waxed keener, and the cold grew with the lengthening days, until the shyest and wildest of the birds from woodland and moor- land flocked under Silvia's window to be fed. Her one great amusement at this time was to keep a good supply of crumbs and broken victuals for the little hungry visitants, and to watch their various

ways. Of all the feathered tribe the robins were the boldest, and the greediest likewise, and their pug- nacity was ah boundless as their appetites; for no sooner did one crimson-vested gentleman secure a treasure to himself, than a brother envied and pro- ceeded to fight him for it; and so it came to pass that many a tough battle did Lady Callerley wit- ness. The blue titmice had souls above crumbs, at least, while there was a morsel of fat to be had, or a bone to be picked; while the yellow-billed black- birds and their sober-looking spouses were shy, but omnivorous in their feeding when no one was near to make them self-conscious. Even the great, clumsy, sable-suited crows waxed tame through hunger, and would come sedately to the ban- quet, turning in their toes as they walked and flapping their wings, with caws of hoarse ecstasy. When this amusement failed the days seemed very long indeed ; for Lady Callerley was not much of a reader, and the fairly good library the house possessed had no attractions for her. Nor did she particularly care for needlework, and indeed it must be confessed that in many respects she was a frivo- lous little creature, with an education_sadly neglected ; and when thrown entirely on her own resources, time was too apt to hang heavily on hand.

She altered the arrangement of her rooms; took down a curtain in one place, and hung up another, moved the stiff furniture about, and scattered a few of the pretty ornaments she possessed, which were mostly wedding presents, on the tables; and in an incredibly short time the formal apartments allotted to her were completely metamorphosed, and rendered infinitely more suitable for the abode of such a bright young lady. Then she held a review of all her finery, and this got through half a day. But what was the use of stylish dresses if there was no one to admire them? As for Lancelot, she was quite sure he never noticed what she wore; in fact some days she wondered whether he noticed her at all, or not.

_ , He was completely absorbed in his duties and forgot that a young bride wants some admiration, or at least some demonstration, from one who ought not to have so quickly merged the lover in the husband. There is only this to be said for Sir Lancelot, that he had been very little of a lover at any time, so that there was not the same falling off there might otherwise have been; only it was surely not altogether unreasonable to hope (if Silvia cherished such a hope) that he might still develop the lover, after becoming the husband. Absorbed as he was, however, he saw at length that the girl, fresh from a gay town life with the gayest of chaperones, was moping and losing her colour and appetite; and he therefore acquiesced delightedly when she herself suggested that his cousin, Mrs. Breamish, and her boy Lance, might now pay them the visit he had spoken of. It was the lad Silvia hankered after, and for whose sake she thought it possible to endure the distasteful company of the mother. The attraction was this, that he was young and gay, and full of life and mischief and if she did not have a playfellow soon she would• certainly be bored to death. Besides, . . . .

they were invited ;and it would be bad taste 6 defer the vitit too long. Dorothy Bree.mish had ever a pang of envy when she entered as 'guest the place wherein she had hoped to reign as mistress ; and now, harassed by debt and with the shadow of coming troubles cast upon her, she quite hated the girl who reigned there in her stead. Of course this was altogether unreasonable, since Silvia had nothing to do either with Mrs. Breamish's blunders in matrimony or failure to attain the height she once attained to. But when was a soured and envious woman capable of reason? Even the affection which sprang up between Lady Callerley and little Lance gave offence to the mother, who was jealous and exacting in her love for her boy, who on his part rather endured her caresses and endearments, than really cared for them. He was of an open candid nature, and his mother's half truths, and occasional lapses into falsehood, roused his indignation, and made him the partisan of a father whom he yould not wholly respect. It was a bad school for the education of a young soul, although, thanks to an ingrained honesty, he had taken slight harm as yet. Mrs. Breamish was at ereat nains to inoratiato herself Iran ner cousin ear iAnceiot, and succeeded to o considerable extent. He set down Silvia's dislike of Dorothy as a small feminine prejudice, arising " partly from a notion altogether erroneous, and an utter incapacity to do justice to a good, but rather unfortunate woman. The Callerleys were, like all trite Ndrthumbrians, "clannish."- That is, they held by their own family through thick and thin, through right and wrong; and therefore Sir Lance- lot"was predisposed to like his cousin, and to look leniently -upon all her actions, even had she not studied hita and suited herself to his varying moods, in a way that surpassed the powers of a young, inexperienced girl like Silvia. If he was conscious of any sCherning or over counsinly affection in the past, he would not admit it. Perhaps he was too modest to allow that any woman had angled for him; perhaps a knowledge of it only caused him to feel a softness towards her. Even the strongest and hardest of men may sometimes be found weak in that respect. She talked of his mother, and of their young days, and he remembered that she had been ever tender and watchful of that mother. After his father's derth she had become a great invalid, and had needed a great deal of care and attention. He was surprised at the thoroughness of his cousin's knowledge of all appertaining to the estate, the wants and requirements of his tenantry, and the different nature of the soil in various parts. So great was the business capacity she showed, and so helpless did he himself feel upon the subjects wherewith she was well acquainted, that he uncon- sciously began to consult her, and to rely upon her judgment in every possible manner. Once or twice it struck him with a sense of wonder, why, since Dorothy Breamish was so clever and sensible a woman, things had been allowed to go so very far amiss at Breamish, as the condition of house and grounds showed to be the case? "There is no doubt that I ought to have returned to the place long ago," said the baronet, thoughtfully, sfterneen „when._ some worry. having crowed

ne naa oeen cuscussmg plans to aneviate It with Madam in the picture gallery; "but surely, you can understand, without many words on my part, how, after my mother was laid to rest, I grew to hate the old home! I vras young then, —and impressionable I suppose, and there were circumstances connected with my father's death which • affected my imagination too vividly. Morbid and melancholy as I then was, there is no knowing how it might all have ended had I re- mained-here. Yes, I did right to leave, to travel,. to get away from all the—the cursed atmosphere of horror and superstition." Sir Lancelot Callerley was evidently much moved by the retrospect in which he was indulging, for he spoke with vehemence, and rapid utterance. Sud- denly he seemed to put a guard on himself, for he stopped, and moved his shoulders with an impatient gesture. Madam watched him furtively. She recalled his mother's dread of the effects upon his mind of what he designated "horror and superstition." Had he indeed got rid of the clinging mists once creeping over his mind, and threatening to overthrow sense and reason? Only second to the love which she had for her boy, her ow& flesh and blood, was the affection Dorothy Breamish, through years of indifference and of absence, yet retained for her cousin Lance' lot. He was her first, indeed it may be said her only love, the one man who had ever aroused a- spark of real passion within her breast. A more commonplace, business-like affair than her marriage could not have been imagined; and now there were times when, if a wish could have killed, the good- natured squire, would have fared badly. Whet ' heart she had was with her cousin. And yet, so strangely is human nature com- pounded of sentiment and selfishness, that the first. thought that came to Dorothy Brea,mish was this. one.
and.

Her boy was heir-at-law of the Callerley estates. Watching Sir Lancelot's deep set. eyes grow som- bre, and a dark brooding expression creep over his face, the woman who fancied she loved him, felt for the instant neither pity nor sorrow. Her own. little Lance might yet be owner of Seaton Callerley, should the present one go Mad from thinking of tha past, and die without issue. This undoubted fact, whispered into her ear by the devil, was dismissed. as rapidly as it had come, but its influence lingered, all the same. _ _ .

" Ah yes, Lancelot; I must needs confess that you had cause to run away from your responsi- bilities," she said slowly. Sir Lancelot glanced at her, as though a sting: lay, in the words. "My responsibilities? True !! It looks cowardly to have shirked them so long. But, never mind! It is not too late to mend."

"Nay, cousin, you make too much of my poor word, 'spoken, I assure you, without thought. W are glad to have you back again, that's all, I °illy- hope—" She broke off here, and sighed. "What/ Speak out Dorothy, I hate hints anel half speeches' you know that of old." "Faith, Lancelot, I scarcely knew what I meant I Your burden has been a heavy one, and. even now the shadow of it has not entirely gone - from you. It would lighten it, methinks, could- you share it with someone! Troubles lose their force to some extent, and presentiments of evil melt frost in sunshine, if they are spoken of to• one whose sympathy and love is entirely your own. Lancelot, for your sake, I am sometimes tempted- to wish your wife were a few years older and—and- -graver. You must not be angry with me for- , saying this, for she is very sweet, and loving, ana I pretty." "Be quiet, Dorothy! Why will you persist ie reminding me of the disparity in our years ? you think it so likely that I should forget the un- pleasant fact that I am old enough to be her father ? " Sir Lancelot spoke with considerable irritation, -and Mrs. Breanush's tact warned her that it was delicate ground upon which she was treading. might have misgivings himself, but that was not to say that the rest of the world need share them.

"She will grow quiet and sober only too soon in this-house," he went on, walking down the goner/ until he reached a window, where he stood, his attention apparently arrested by something outside. "Is it not and to have something young, and bright, and joyous, to turn to for hope and comfort, when one feels life too sad, and fate too threat- ening?" Mrs. Breamish followed him down, and she also paused, and looked out. The window opened upon a courtyard, where a great solid mass of snow had fallen and accumu- lated, by avalanches from the roofs and outbuild- ings. Lady Callerley and Lance were here to be seen, very busily employed ; and shouts of laughter and merriment ascended to the spectators. The two comrades had built a huge snow man, a regular Frankenstein, and were now adding to him finish- ing touches, in the shape of hat, and gloves, and. pipe. A smile crept around the corners of Sir Lancelot's lips, as he watched the fun. Silvia, wrapped up in furs, with little of her face to be discerned save a pair of laughing eyes and a. rosy mouth, yet suggested something sweet and in- effably lovable ; and with a bitter pang of jealousy, Madam noted a change come over Sir Lancelot, as he followed with his eyes every movement Of the young and graceful girl he had made his wife. But Mrs. Breamish was too clever a woman to commit one of the commonest blunders of her sex ; and to show her hand, for the sake of indulging bi a spiteful remark. " What a pretty little Lady Callerley it is Out there in the snow," she remarked in a pleasant tone. "A very child, innocent and light-hearted, forgetful of all but the moment's en- joyment. yes, Lancelot, you were in the right to choose her. ." It must indeed be pleasant to own a creature so joyous and bright as that. I congratu- late you upon your child wife." • (To be continued).

div.head: SINGULAR GUN ACCIDENT,--A CHILD
div.p: SINGULAR GUN ACCIDENT,--A CHILD
SHOT BY A DOG.

A singular gun accident has been the subject of fil" quiry before the coroner at Carlton-on-Trent. A farmer in that neighbourhood named Marrison, being about to shoot rabbits, took down an old-fashioned muzzle-loader gun from the wall of his kitchen, and observing that the caps looked damp laid the weapon on the table while be went to a cupboard for a box of caps. According r° the evidence, his back had not been turned more than el minute when a dog entered the room playfully, aliel scratching with his paws upon the table somehow col: trived to move the trigger. An explosion instantly f° lowed, and unhappily an infant child of the farmer, ittle boy, aged six, who was standing by his moth it side near the Ilre, was shot through the head, and fel/ dead. On examining the table, a black mark was fontt where the cap had exploded, besides a groove on th' surface of the table caused by the passage of the sh°t` The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

"Very well, dear. lam sorry to hear about the busi- ness ; how do you account for it 2" "Oh! more competition, and the profits cut closer than ever. lam sure I don't know what it is going to end in."

We suppose it would be hard to find a family where a , conversation very like the above has not taken place ' some time or other, and with many it is an oft-repeated Story. div.head: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETINGS IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETINGS IN WARRINGTON.
SPEECHES BY MR. It. PIERPOINT.

• the first of a series of Conservative Ward meet• ings was held on Monday evening, in St. Barnabas' §chool, the meeting being for the purpose of elect- Lug chairman, vice-chairmen, &c., for Whitecross Ward. Mr.A.Woods presided,and he was supported on the platform by Mr. R. Pierpoint, the Conserva- tive candidate, Mr. W.H. Cookson, and Mr.J.Hamp- son (Conservative agent). ZLEOTION OF OFFICERS. DISCARDING A TOWN
COUNCILLOR.

_ Mr. A. Woods was re-elected chairman of the Ward. The chairman said the vice-chairmen last Year were Mr. It, T. Smith, Councillor L. Greening, arld Mr. W. Bellian. Mr. Houghton said he wouid znove the re-election of these, with the exception of ecumeillo! Greening. This proposal was seconded and agreed to without further remark. Mr. Cook- -4011 was re-elected secretary, and the captains and Other officials were also appointed. SIR GILBERT CREENALL AND WHITECROSS WARD.

The CHAIRMAN referred to the coming retirement of Sir Gilbert Greenall, and he added that Sir Gilbert had taken an enormous interest in Whitecross ward because he had always been given to understand that it was one of those blots of Liberalism which could not be wiped ()tit. He suggested that he should write a letter to Sir Gilbert expressing the feelings of the meeting with re- gard to himselt, and this suggestion was agreed to. CRITICISM OF DR. HOUSTON'S ADDRESS. Mr. R. PIERPOINT, who was well received, said he was glad to say that since he last had the opportunity of ap- Pearing in public their oppoaents had chosen a candi- date, and he was glad to think that they had chosen a Irian who, from what he had been told and had seen in the newspapers, was a man, stranger though he was, Whom they might welcome as an opponent, and who I;asi he trusted, an honourable and straightforward man. Re wished to say that he hoped the ensuing election would be carried through from the beginning to the end asa clear upstanding fight, with no hard personal things Said about one or the other, so that though they might differ absolutely in politics they might respect each other as opponents. (Applause.) Still, he trusted that Would not prevent them saying what they liked about tbe political principles which they held. (Hear. hear.) He found that his opponent had made a long speech of considerable ability, but there was one thing he particu- larly wished to emphasise, and that was that he very Properly nut the question of Home Rule first in his Programme, but having put it first he gave it What he called a " half-holiday." That was, having pro- duced it he immediately left it-in the condition in which he found it. He simply said that the democracy of Ire- land had grasped the hand of the democracy of England, and would not let it go. It was the old story of the union Of hearts. But they wanted to know a great deal more than that about Home Rule. They wanted to know 'whether the old Bill of 1886 is alive or it is dead. They Wanted to know whether the Irish members of Parlia- t,?_ent, if they had a Parliament in Dublin, were to sit in Parliament of Westminster, and if they are, why they are to sit in two Parliaments ? (Hear, hear.) They Ilso wanted to know whether the customs and excise Were to be put in the hands of the Irish Government, be, cause it was rather a serious question for the trade of -Tingland if the Irish wete allowed to put prohibitory tariffs on English goods. They also wanted to know if the Irish Government were to have the appointment of tile judges and if the police were to be in their hands. They•o repeated that, above all they wanted to know if the Loille Rule Bill of 1886 was dead.—Mr. PIERPOINT said ,'"" Position reminded him of the following story. One 'day a certain Patrick O'Brien was walking through a ,ve-yard and he saw a tombstome upon which were the words " Weep not for me my parents dear, I am not dead but sleeping here," and Patrick said " If I Was dead I would not be ashamed to own it." (Loud , tanghter.) There was another thing they wanted to find out, and that was whether Ulster was to be included in this grand scheme, for if it was they /8,h,...0u1d have a great deal to say about that in England. (Rear, hear.) Dealing with other points in Dr. Hous- ton's address Mr. Pierpoint said the cry of reducing the duration of 'Parliament never took place when Mr. Gladstone was in office. As to the payment of mem- bers of Parliament, it had been asked by a very great 111, an, that while they had a very large number of fit and vroper persons ready to take office in Parliament for nothing, why should the country be taxed to pay them. (Rear, hear.) The great man whom he quoted was Mr. ladstorie. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 16, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 16, 1892.
MILK PROSECUTION AT ST. HELENS.

A CHESHIRE FARMER HEAVILY FINED. At the St. llelens Town Hall, on Friday, before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair, Thomas Prescott, of the Stocks Farm, Wimboldsley, hear Middle-viol], was summoned for supplying adul- terated milk. The proceedings were instituted by Chief Constable Wood, and Mr. Robert Bygott (Messrs. Robert Bygott and Sons, Middlewich) defended. Mr. J. P. Mearns (St. Helens) watched the case on behalf of seve- ral local milk dealers who were interested in the pro- ceedings.—The evidence showed that for some years Jas.Webb, a milk dealer, residing in Duke-st., St.Helens, had received his supply of milk on Sunday mornings from the defendant. On the 20th December Police-inspector Steele was at the railway station when the milk arrived, and took samples of it. On the following day these were handed over to Dr. Campbell Brown, of Liverpool, who analysed the milk, and certified that it con- tained upwards of six parts of water, which had been added to every 100 parts of milk. Dr. Campbell Brown attended at the court to give evidence, and said that the results of his analysis were calculated on the supposition that the milk was originally of the poorest quality ever yielded by cows. As the milk was apparently not of that low quality originally, the quantity of water added had probably been greater than that naraed, but he could not say definitely, as he always calcu- lated on the supposition that it was the poorest milk. Witness : All falsehoods die hard, but I have proved the fact by experiment.—Mr. Bygott, for the defence, first took a technical objection to the proceedings on the ground that the offence was not specifically stated on the information, as required by the Food and Drugs Act. —The Bench overruled the contention.—Mr. Bygott strongly denied that any water had been added, and said it was forwarded to St.Helens in exactly the same condition as it was when received from the cow.—Evi- dence in support of Mr. Bygott's statement was given by the defendant and one of his servants named Mary Holbrook. After a consultation, the Bench imposed a fine °ILI and costs, and :ordered the defendant to pay the fees and expenses of the analyst amounting to £3 10s. The total amount was £5 10s.

div.head: LATE STATIONMASTER AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: THE LATE STATIONMASTER AT LATCHFORD.

The addiess which is to be presented to Mr. Joseph Harrison, formerly stationmaster at Latch- ford, is now on view in the shop window of Mr. Blackhurst, jeweller, Sankey-et., Warrington, it has been most artistically illuminated by Messrs. Brookes and Sons, of Warrington,and the frame is an ex- ceptionally handsome one. The text is as follows : Latchford, Cheshire, January, 1892. Mr. Joseph Harrison, Lime-street Station, Liverpool. On your leaving Latchford, where you have so ably performed your duties of stationmaster for the last 14 years, to take your new appointment of night stationmaster at Lime-street, Liverpool, it was resolved at a me'Aing held at Latchford, that your courtesy, kindness, and ability should be substantially recognised. And we have great pleasure, en behalf of the inhabitants of Latch- ford and neighbourhood and ourselves of testifying the same by our signatures to this memorial, and by pre- senting you with a purse containing 40 guineas. We congratulate the London and North-Wastern Railway Company in having such a good servant, and wishing you every success in your new position, whilst regrett- ing the loss of you at Latchford.—We are, dear sir, yours, faithfully, Percy Davies and Henry toberts,joint secretaries ; Edward Greenall, jun., Mayor of Warring - ton, treasurer." The date of the presentation has not been fixed.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT LATCHFORD. On Monday afternoon an inquest was held at the Ship Canal Hospital, Latchford, on the body of a labourer on the Canal named Matthew Cawley. The deceased, who was 35 years of age, and a native of Liverpool, was on his way to dinner on Friday afternoon last, when he was knocked down by an engine, and so seriously injured that he died the same day, at the Hospital, to which he had been removed. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased, at the time of the accident, which took place near the Hospital, at Latchford, was hurrying to a special pumping station at the bottom of the Canal, where there was a fire. Ile was unconscious when picked up. His injuries had been inflicted by a crank, the engine having passed over him. A verdict of "Acci- dental death" was returned. Mr. H. C. Yates was the coroner.

div.head: MINERS' CONFERENC,F..
div.p: MINERS' CONFERENC,F..

Mr. S. Woods, presiding on Wednesday over the Miners' Federation Conference at Stoke-on-Trent, said the membership had increased from 36,000 in 1888 to 178,513 in 1802. The aggregate capital of their various associations amounted to half-a-million sterling. He declared the Federation to be against sliding scales, as they encouraged reductions in prices of coal. He denied that there was any depression in the coal trade, seeing that the output had steadily increased during the past five years. He advocated an increased effort to secure the Eight Hours Bill and the return of workmen to Parliament. It was unanimously resolved to resist any reduction in wages.

div.head: ALLEGED ANARCHIST PLOT,
div.p: ALLEGED ANARCHIST PLOT,

John Westley, brushmaker, a member of the Walsall Socialist Club, was arrested at Walsall on Tuesday, charged with complicity in the anarchical plot which has been engaging the attention of the authorities. On Wednesday William Ditchfield flame, described as a filer, was apprehended at Walsall on a charge of being concerned, with four other men already in custody, in an Anarchist plot. An Italian named John Batto alica Desganaviety, was also arrested in Charlotte-st., Soho, London. It is stated that a fully charged bomb has been discovered in Parliament Hill-fields, between Hampstead and Highgate.

A man, named Evans, lost his life on Tuesday in a fire in Dynham-road, West Hampstead, London. Four valuable horses were burned to death on Toes day, in the stables of Messrs. Wall and Co.. Bolton. The Bishop of Liverpool, in the cours e of a letter to a member of a Russo-Jewish local appeal committee, ex- presles stroryz disapproval of the persecution Jews are suffering in Russia,and offers to forward a subscription.

TOLLEMACTIE, M.P., SOUNDS A NOTE OF ALARM.

Speaking at Sandiway, in Mid-Cheshire, at a Prim- rose League meeting, Mr. Henry Tollemache, M.P.,said he viewed with the greatest apprehension the proposal which it was said the Government were going to bring forward of local government for Ireland. He was in favour of local government for Ireland just as much as for England, but before it was given, Irishmen ought to behave themselves as well as Englishmen and Scotch- men did. Irehtnd, he thought, was not ripe for local government, and unless there were sufficient safeguards introduced—and of the efficacy of those safeguards he had very grave doubts—he for one would be no party to supporting such a measure, although it might be pro- posed by Lord Salisbury's Government.

The Clerk then read a communication as to the amount for which the County Council would un- dertake the repair of certain reads as main roads, namely from Budworth Hollow to the junction with Chester and Warrington main road at the end of Wilaerspool Causeway being a length of seven miles three furlongs and the road from a junction with Chester and Warrington main road at Acton Grange to Runcorn omitting that part of the road maintained by the Norton Estate being a length of two miles seven fur- longs.-1 he Chairman took strong exception to what he considered the heavy conditions laid down by the eounty Council. He had told the Committee of the County Council on this question being discussed that thoy had better decline to take them over at once.— Mr. Darbyshire said to launch into such an exorbitant expenditure as the County Council named would be simply ridiculous.—The Chairman proposed that the County Council be informed, that their conditions were unacceptable, and begging re-consideration of the mat- ter.—Mr. Long seconded the resolution, and it was un- animously carried. THE SHIP CANAL CO'S BILL.
The Clerk reported that this Bill did not affect the Board to any extent. There was no occasion for the Board to take any notice of it.

AwNEW ,ROAD. • The Clerk read a report from the Ship' Canal Co rn- mittee as to the construction by the Canal Company of a road from Walton Arches to Moore turnbridge on to the old quay works at Runcorn. The Committee recom- mended the Board to accept a road of 30 feet in width from fence to fence, of which 25 feet must be metalled, and the other 5 feet on the South side formed in to a footpath with suitable curbs, the whole of the work to be finished to the satisfaction of the Board's surveyor by June 24th, 1893, and that the temporary bridges remain as they are until the works are finished for the use of the public.—The report was adopted.—This was all the business of importance.

" AW'LL WED, IF HOO'LL POLISH MI SHOON !" Ther's a Bachelor here, in eawr village, Wo wants to get wed, if he eon; An' if ther's a woman ull soot him, Hoo may settle it neaw—he's her mon ! Hoo'll find him a very nice Messmate, But hoo'll hey to be up rayther soon ; Per i' one thing he's very perticler— He'll want her to polish his shoes! Hoo may oather be steaut or be slender, An' hoo'll do, whether swarthy or leet ; But in case hoo's a fancy fer He'd liefer hoo hadn't big feet ! He wudn't object if her face war As reawnd as a jolly full moon, • If hoo'll only jump up in a mornin', An' gradely weel polish his shoon ! He's a chap that it's easy to pleeuz, An' he's very good tempert an' aw ; Per, if hoo's indium& to boss him, He'll let her ha' plenty o' law. He'll be thankfu' fer aw that hoo cooks him, An' eyt it wi' knife or wi' spoon, So long as hoo sticks to his bargain, An' gets up to polish his shoon Neaw an' then, he'd be off to a Theetre, An' tak' her an' aw, if hoo'd go; Or, if hoo'd prefer it, he'd trayt her I'th' Fair, to th' Zoologikin Show. Ey'ry yer, too, thay'd bathe i' sant wayter, At Seauthpoort or Blackpool i' June; 4 But— hoo'd hey to be careful 6th train tone, An' neglekt noan to polish his shoos ! He'll gie her his brass Wry wick eend, An' let her hey wot hoo's amind ; See nowt but wot's reet in her dooin's, An' to aw her fauts he'll be blind; Wen her bread hoo begins to be bakin', He'll help her to put it i'th' boon, So lung ez hoo ne'er disappints him, Wi rizin' to polish his shoon! He'll never be eawt late at neet time, An' seldom get " ovver the line "; An' he wain't wobble worn like a felly, That's fund summut wrung wi' his spine. He'll tak' her to church ey'ry Sunday, An' jine her i'th' chant or i'th' tune ; If, providin' hoo keeps to his contract, An' ne'er fails to polish his shoon! Well, Hurmun, owd lad, here's mi blessin' On thee an' thi wife, wen yo're wed; An' aw hope that thea.u'l ne'er ha' to rue it, Nor feel a rough fist at thi' yed ! May yo allus be happy together, An' wedlock prove nowt but a boon; Wile fer mony a lung year may hoo bless this Wi' childre to polish thi shoots! TUM 0' PEGS.
Nyowton God bless o' 15, 1892.

div.head: RIINCORN.SIVINGS BANK.
div.p: RIINCORN.SIVINGS BANK.
ANNUAL MEETING.

_ The =nal meeting of the trustees and managers of this bank was held at the bank,High-st.,on Tues- day afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P.,the president, occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance. . The minutes of the last meeting having been con- firmed, The Actuary (Mr. W. Handley) read the following re- port :-The year's account commenced on the debtor 1 side with a sum of £29,469 13s. id. (being the amount due to depositors £29,381 18s. 2d., and the surplus of £B7 14s. 11d.) During the year there have been received the following sums: Depositors in money,£B.l4o us. 2d.; transfers from Post:.Office Savings Bank, £2olos. Id. transfers from other savings bank, £66 Bs. 6d; interest from National Debt Commissioners, £791 is. sd. ; divi- dends on Governmestlstock, £2B 3s. 9d. ; sale of stock for depositors, £95 Os. 3d. ; commission on purchase ' of stock. 75. 6d. ; sale of bank pass books, £1 12s. 10d. ; total, £38,613 Bs. 7d. On the credit side there has been paid to depositors during the year in money, £8,859 Os. Bd. ; depositors for £3OO consol stock purchased, £287 lie. 9d. ; management expenses, £9O 17s. 3d. ; invested with the National Debt Commissioners, £29,008 12s. Bd. ; in the hands of the treasurer, £367 6s. 3d. ; total, £38,613 Bs. 7d. After adding the sum of £723 15s. 4d. as interest and dividends to de- positors accounts the ledger balance was £29,281 lie. Id., which sum deducted from the amount in the hands of the treasurer and National Debt Commissioners show the Bank surplus to be £94 7s. 10d. an increase for the year of £6 12s. 11d. The number of I separate deposits dnring the year had been 2,419 and of withdrawals 914 ; a total of 3,333 separate transactions and a turnover in money of £16,999 11s. 10d., an increase over last year of £435 7s. 2d. The amount deposited by the various societies was £1,632 15s. 2d., and the amount withdrawn £2,118 11s. Bd. Excluding these sums the average deposit per member had been £2 18s. 3d. and the average withdrawel £8 12s. 9d. The number of open accounts at the commencement of the Bank year was 1,029; at the close, 1,065 ; an increase of 38. Of the total number of accounts the balances of more than one half do not exceed £lO each, the average being slightly under £2 10s. The stock account showed a net increase for the year of £2OO. At the commence- ment the amount stood at £9OO • £3OO additional having been purchased and £lOO sold, tire present amount being ,Cl,lOO. It would have been noticed that the ledger balances were about £lOO less than at the close of last year. This was fully accoanted for by the fact that the accounts of the various societies were £4OO less than at the close of last year's accounts. In several cases considerable amounts had been withdrawn for invest- ments yielding a larger return than the bank rate. Per- sonal deposits had,however' exceeded last year's amount by no less a sum than £1,150, while personal with- drawals had only exceeded last year by £337, and of this amount £287 had been withdrawn for investment in good stock, and a considerable further amount had been withdrawn for the purchase of cottage property, facts which bear out testimony to the usefulness of the Bank in promoting habits of thrift and in making pro- visions for future days. The treasurer had so carefully watched over the financial affairs of the Bank that the interest or treasurer's balances had so nearly approxim- ated to the commission as to have only entailed a cost 3s. 10d. on a turnover of nearly £17,000. The certifi- cates of the National Debt Commissioners and the trea- surer for the amounts held by them respectively and also the certificate of the auditors as to the examina- tion of the books and accounts were produced. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, expressed the pleasure he derived from attending the annual meeting of the Bank, especially as it was one of the institutions that continued to flourish and extend its usefulness in Runcorn. He noticed from the balance sheet and report, that the general amount of business had been more than usual, and the number of accounts was also greater, after allowing for all that had been closed during the year. The deposits of individual mem- bers had been about £1,150 in excess of the previous year. One other feature struck him forcibly, and that was that some accounts had been transferred from the Post Office Savings Bank to their bank, a fact that showed the public had complete confidence in the management. He thought this spoke well for the position the bank held or had held so long in the town. The Chairman also drew attention to the valuable services rendered by the treasurer, Mr. John Simpson, who had only incurred a charge of 3s. 10d. for the large turnover of the bank. This spoke well for the great interest Mr. Simpson took in the Bank.-The Rev. Dr. Preston seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. Dr. Preston proposed and Mr. F. A. Lake seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Simpson for his services as trea- surer during the past year, and it was carried unanim- ously. The thanks of the trustees and managers were also accorded to the auditors on the motion of Mr. E. Imison seconded by Mr. John Littler.-Mr. Thomas Handley proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, remarking that Mr. Brundrit filled the position of presid- ent to the bank as he filled every other public position he undertook, with dignity and thoroughness. The motion was seconded by Dr. Preston. In replying, the Chairman said he thought they were greatly indebted to the Actuary for the way in which he managed the bank, as shown by the continued interest taken in its affairs year after year. The Actuary was thanked without a formal vote and the proceedings terminated.
FATALITIES AT AN ARRI NGTO N.
SUDDEN DEATH OF A LABOURER.

Patrick Glynn, aged 66, bricklayers' labourer, who lodged at No. 4. Dallam-lane, died at 8-30 on Saturday night, under the following circumstances: —Deceased had suffered from bronchitis for years, and had had medicine frequently from the In. firm- ary, until six weeks ago. Ile had been out of em- ployment for the past five weeks, and had very little to live upon, except what his sister, who is a cook, gave him. On Thursday he went to the Old Men's Dinner, at the Public Hall. On Friday he was very ill, and said he would not live many days. He drank some rum, and as he became weaker, the landlady sent fer a priest, who recommended him to send for a doctor. This, however, he failed to do, and died at the time stated. No inquest has been held.

A FALL AND ITS RESULTS. An inquest was held at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay, on Monday, by Mr. W. T. Husband, on the body of Wm. Massey, aged 64, and who used to reside with his daughter, Ann Blackwood, in Fac- tory-lane. It appeared from the evidence given that the deceased was at the inn above-named on the 29th ult., and had two glasses of port wine. He left before six o'clock, but as he was going out, he slipped on the pavement. One of the witnesses,Mr. Smith, picked him up, with the assistance of Miss Dutton,the landlord's daughter. It was found that he was bleeding from the right ear. He was taken home in a cab. Dr. Kisby was called in, and at- tended him till his death, which took place on Fri- day. The deceased's daughter said that her father was subject to " mazy bouts." B.e had been a tee- totaller for ten years.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned.

A FATAL FALL IN THE MARKET PLACE. Yesterday morning an inquest was held by Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, concerning the death of Rachael Smith, aged 82, who resided with her married daughter, at No. 2, Egerton-st. The deceased's- daughter, Elizabeth Gibson said her mother was insured in the Prudential dub for £l2 and in a " noggin " club. The Saturday before Christmas week the deceased 'went out and I had a fall as she subsequently told her, on the Mar- ket Hall steps, and hurt her leg, and was also severely shaken. She was taken to the Infirmary, where she died on Wednesday, the 7tn inst., about a quarter to six in the morning.—Sarah Enness, 20, Old-st., said on the Saturday before Christmas, she saw the deceased slip on the steps of the Market Hall, and helped her up, She was afterwards con- veyed to the Infirmary.—The verdict was acciden- tal death.
