div.head: EDUCATION.
div.p: EDUCATION.

A meeting of Conservatives of Latchford Ward, was held in St. James's Sehool, Old-road, on Wednesday evening. Councillor W. Tinsley presided, and opened the proceedings. He was supported on the platform by Councillor Greening, Mr. John Hartley, secretary to the Ward committee, Messrs. W. Wallace. J. H. Clarke, R. C. Cooper, Stansfield, S. Reynolds, John Lee, Thomas Knight. Thomas Hankey, and Peter Lamb, and others. Councillor Tinsley was re-elected chairman for the ward for the ensuing year ; and the following were appointed vice-chairmen :—Messrs. John White,W. Jones,D. Jones, J. Davies, E. Greenall, John Les, S. Reynolds, and John Coxon, Alderman Harrison, and Councillors Greening and Ashton. Mr. Hartley was re-appointed secretary, and the captains and committee were also elected. The chairman read a letter from Alderman Chandley, regretting his inability to be present. He hoped that the Conservatives of the district would do what they could to cancel the injury now being done to this country by the talented but treacherous man, W. E. Gladstone. Mr. R. PIERPOINT then addressed the meeting. He claimed to belong to the good old-fashioned Tory party, and believed that he was on the right side. It seemed to him rather strange that an Irish gentleman aspiring to get into Parliament should not put himself forward for a constituency on the other side ot the channel. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that he himself as an Englishman, and especially a Warrington man, had in some degree a better claim. -(Applause.) Referring to the Newcastle pro- gramme Mr. Pierpoint said he did not particularly object to one man one vote, provided that the measure was coupled with a re-distribution of seats. In this re-distribution 13 to 18 seats would have to be taken from Ireland and put to England. In England and Scotland the illiterate voters amounted to some 14 per cent., and in Ireland to about 154 per cent. He could not conceive that because a country was in the enjoyment of less education than another, therefore it should be more represented. The Gladstonians had vapoured for a great imam* years about free education, and who had carried it? Lord Salisbury and his Government. (An elector here asked how it was that he had to pay for his children's school- ing, if there was free education.) He, Mr. Pierpoint, said he really could not enter into details, but he thought he was right in his statement. (The elector : I know I have to pay for my chilcren going to school.) Mr. Pierpoint : You have ! (The elector : Yes, certainly.) He was sorry the gentlemen disagreed with him, but he could not help it. He was in favour of compensation to publicans whose licenses were taken away from them without fault on their part. The remainder of Mr. dierpoint's speech for the most part was devoted to Home Rule.
A vote approving the selection of Mr. Pierpoint. as a 'candidate was then adopted on the motion of Councillor Greening and Mr. Pierpoint having thanked the meeting,
it conclti'ded.

div.head: TOWN HALL WARD.
div.p: TOWN HALL WARD.

The meeting of AConservatives fer7t-he.Town Hall Ward took place on Thursday night, in St. Paul's Girls' school- room. Councillor J. Smethurst presided, and there were also on the platform Mr. R. Pierpoint (Conserva- tive candidate), Major Nicholson; Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins, A. Bennett, J. Hampson kConservative agent). Amongst the letters of apology for non-attendance was one from Councillor R. Heaton who wrote that he hoped that the town would be represented by a townsman and not by a foreigner. The following ward officers were appointed :—Chairman, Councillor J. Smethurst; vice- chairmen, Mr. E. Ackland, and Mr. A. J. Jolley; secre- tary, Mr. J. Gibson. The captains and ward committees were also elected. It was decided that, owing to the death of the Duke of Clarence, no political speeches should be made. A resolution as, however, passed with reference to the death of His Royal Highness, and will be found in another column.
RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY

AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Dutton Union Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. J. Mclntyre (chairman), Weir, Baguley, Aaron,lieywood, Lewis, Pickering, Parr, Whitlow, Brett' erton, Baxter,M oun- field, Brandreth, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. Farrington (inspector). THE SIIIP CANAL COMPANY'S BILL.

The Clerk said he had, as instructed at last meeting, obtained a copy af the Bill which the Ship Canal Com- pany proposed to promote in next Parliament, and which had been deposited in different parts of the Union. Although the Bill sought power to repeal some parts of the Act of 1885, it did not seem to effect that Authority at all. The Ship Canal Company gave the Authority notice an account of the latter' sewer outfalls.-0 n the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Weir, the Clerk was instructed to watch the bill of the Ship Canal Com- pany, to see whether it was going to affect any sewers belonging to the Authority.
THE DOCTOR LAID UP WITH INFLUENZA.
The Clerk read a letter from the daughter of Dr. Adams, the medical officer, stating that as he was suffer- ing from influenza he was unable to be present.
THE IMPURITY OF THE MERSEY AND IRWELL.

The Inspector read a report prepared by way of reply to a circular letter addressed to the Authority on Nov- ember 2nd last by a joint committee of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils for carrying into effect the provisions of the Rivers Pollution (Prevention) Act, 1878, within the watershed of the rivers Mersey and Ir- well. The Committee had informed the Authority that they had concluded that the time had now arrived when in the interests of the health and comfort of the com- munity steps should be taken without delay to purify the rivers. The Inspector in his reply stated that during 1884, with a view to the entorcement of the Act, one of the canals passing through the Authority's district and which at the time was a combination of the rivers in question, and canal, being in an offen- sive condition through being largely polluted with sewage, &e., the Authority directed him to make an inspection of the said rivers and canal running between Runcorn and Manchester, when it was found that by far the greater quantity of sewage and poison. ous liquid came from towas and other places situate in the Lancashire side little or nothing in comparison com- ing in from the other side. As nothing could be accom- plished without the co-operation of the other Authorities in the enforcement of the provisions of the Act, the project was abandoned. since the formation of the sanitary district, two sewage schemes had been carried out, in both of which the sewage discharged into a tidal portion of the river Mersey, one in a direct, and the other in an indirect manner. In both cases the sanction of the Board of Trade was obtained. The adoption of both schemes had without a doubt had a beneficial effect upon the health of the community in the immediate neighbourhoods where they had been adapted. The Authority had no scheme of sewerage in contemplation at present—lt was decided that a copy of the - art be sent to the joint committee of the County Cr wisMENTs.

div.head: WOMAN BURNED TO DEATII.
div.p: A WOMAN BURNED TO DEATII.

Mr. Husband then held an inquest as to the death of Annie Pargetter, of 7, Water-street, Latchford, wife of John William Pargetter, employed at the rubber works, who died under the following tragical circumatances.—The deceased's husband said she was aged 56 years. On the 14th of November she got badly burnt. He saw her about 20 minutes after the accident. She had been reading the newspaper to him, by the fire, shortly before the accident. He went straight for a doctor. When he got back she was in a cab, and he went with her to the Infirmary. The next morning she said she had had a fainting bout, but could not say how she came by the burns. She had been subject to fits.—Sarah Baguley, a neigh- bour of the deceased, said about half-past eight on the night of the 14th,she heard the deceased moan- ing in her house,and went in and found her behind the door with her clothing on fire fiom her feet to her shoulders. She threw her to the lloor,and tried to put out the flames, but Thos. Sutton came in and put out the fire, and P.C. Dean came, and she was taken to the Infirmary. Witness had left her sitt- ing by the fire about a quarter of an hour before the accident happened.—Emily Dobson, nurse at the Infirmary, deposed that the decased was ad- mitted there on November 14th, and died there on Tuesday morning last, from the effects of the burns. —A verdict of Accidantal death was returned.

div.head: PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE
div.p: THE PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE
FOR RUNCORN.

A special meeting of Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners was held on Thursday,under the presidency of Mr. H. J. Grice. There were present Messrs. H. White, E. W. Humphreys' J. Pritchard, J. Meadow- ernf t, P. Wiewall, J. W. Lightburn, 11. Coward, R. Abel, P. Smith, D. Bisbrown, W.R.Wass,W. Hankin- son F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), andM. Barker (surveyor). The business was to re- ceive the following recommendations of the Par- liamentary and Legal Committee :—That the plan of Mr. Bowden, C,E., of a Technical Institute, marked No. 1, , be adopted, and subject to such alterations in detail as may be deemed advisable. That Mr. Bowden be in- structed to prepare detail drawings and specifications to submit to the Department of Science and Art, with a. view to obtaining a grant. That a copy of Mr Bowden's plan and report, with a copy of the foregoing resolutions, be submitted to the Cheshire County Council,with aview to obtaining a building grant. Mr. Pritchard asked the Law Clerk whether it was his duty as chairman of the Committee to propose these motions seeing that he differed from them.—The Law Clerk said it was not a matter of law. In his opinion it was not the duty af any man to move the adoption of any recommendation +nr resolution contrary to his opin- ions. If a chairman differed from the majority of his Committee on a matter of principle or of great import- ance, it was a question between the Committees and himself as to his posision.—Mr. Pritchard said that was contrary to the opinion expressed by a member last week.—Mr. Lightburn said he recognised fully Mr. Lake's opinion on any legal question, but he must allow him (Mr. Lightburn) to differ from him on what he con- sidered the unwritten law in regard to the Committee of that Board. The Chairman of a Committee was supposed to obey the behests of the Committee, at the same time reserving the right to differ from it. If he felt himself out of touch with a Committee on I • essential points he should take it into serious I consideration whether he should resign or not. Mr. ' Lightburn then moved the adoption of the recommenda- tion, and answering the question how they were to maintain the Institution, said there were four sources of maintenance—the penny rate £195, the grant from the County Council, which might be considered artain £220 school fees from pupils, and the grant from the science and art department on the passes of students. As to how the money was to be found to build the Institute, there was a building grant from the Scienee and Art Department, the maximum of which was £l,OOO ; there was the unappropriated balance in the hands of the County Council, there were private donations, and there would be the balance from two years rates and two years grants from the County Council. They had also the power to mortgage the penny rate to the extent they might require to complete the building. Mr. Bowden estimated the cost at £3,500, but people who knew the wages in Runcorn and the cost of material there were ef opinion that it could be done for between £3,000 and £3,500.-1n answer to Mr. Humphreys the Law Clerk said if the grants from the Department of Science and Art and the County Council were so small as not to justify the Board in going to the full extent of these plans and it would be quite open to them to alter the plans.—Mr. Humphreys under those circumstances seconded the motion.—Mr. Pritchard said he moved the resolution in favour of the Board adopting the Technical Instruction Act so that he could claim to be as enthusi- astic as any member upon this question of technical education. At the same time he could not support these recommendations because he considered the scheme too elaborate and too costly. The cost of the proposed Institute, with furniture would be £5,000, and he wished to know if such a building could be maintained upon £l9O a year, because the grant from the County Council was not certain. As to second- ary education the Board had no funds orpower to estab- lish a secondary school. Now the School Board had the power to levy a rate for a higher grade or secondary. I The School Board would soon have to spend £4,000 for educational purposes and the ratepayers would soon be taxed 6d. in the £ or more for education. He moved that the matter be referred back to the Committee.—Mr. Smith seconded.—Mr. Meadowcroft said having regard to the cost of the building he could not approve of the scheme.—Mr. Wiswall said he thought the building could be put up for £3,000.—on the Law Clerk stating that the question of site could enter into the discussion, Mr. Humphreys withdrew his seconding and the chairman seconded the motion. After a long discussion the amendment was lost, only Messrs. Prit- chard, Smith and White, voting for it.—Mr. Meadow. croft then moved an amendment fixing Mr. Bowden's charge for the plans at £2O, but it received no seconder. The motion was then carried by eight votes to four,those voting in the minority being Messrs. Pritchard, Meadow- croft,-Smith and White.—Mr. Humphreys did not vote Mr. Humphries drew attention to the fact that the County Council was paying the railway fares of pupil teachers and others to attend free technical classes at Chester, and be understood that 40 or fifty intended to to take advantage of the privilege. This was a matter 7hich would require the careful attention of the Board, the County Council was going to enter into competil an with their own classes.—The Chairman said the subject could be discussed when they came to a final decision as to a technical school.

LORD BEACONSFIELD Of blessed Under Which Flag? Primrose memory once described Conservatism as the mule of politics which engenders nothing. Measured by this standard, Mr. Robert PIE RPOINT who aspires to the honour of representing Warrington in Par- liament would seem to be a typical Conservative. During the past week, he has delivered at petty meetings a series of speeches which have been full of petty criticism, but, Conservative to the backbone, they have engendered nothing. Even as to his criticism Mr. PIE RPOINT is curiously out of date. Where can he have been and what can he have been doing during the past few years that he should deal with the Home Rule contro- versy by citations of something Mr. BRIGHT or Mr. W. H. SMITH said that has already become ancient history? He began on Monday night with a story which meant, if it meant anything, that Home Rule was dead; but by Tuesday night he had so far changed his mind as to come to the conclusion that the next election would be con- tested on the Home Rule issue. This is undoubt- edly true, but it is only a portion of the truth. English electors have made up their minds to give Ireland an opportunity of managing her own domestic affairs in her own way ; and they are not tobe influenced in the matter by " shreds and patches" df quotations from speeches and pam- phlets which have already become musty. They are for doing justice to Ireland, and, more than that, they are for seeing that justice is done to themselves. Dr. flousTort as the Liberal candidate recognises this ; and he advocates a programme which at once commends itself to the mass of the people.

What does Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT offer on the other side? Nothing—absolutely nothing. He in- dulges in criticism which to the elector, hungering for redress of grievances, is about as cheerful and as filling as the east wind. Working-men will know what to think of the applicant for their suffrages who contemptuously dismisses the Eight Hours Bill and the proposal to shorten Parliaments. He says the Septennial Act is good enough for him, and thinks it to the purpose to affirm that the cry for shortening Parliaments was never heard of when Mr. GLADSTONE was in office. What if that were so ? Would it affect the wisdom or the justice of the proposal? But it is not true that the demand for shorter Parliaments is a new thing; it was put forward by Reformers in the Chartist days of fifty years ago; and it has been advocated ever since, until now the stage is reached when it is being specially supported by Liberals and specially opposed by Tories. Another point of what used to be called "the Charter," is "payment of members:' Mr. PIERPOINT, as a rich man, will have nothing to do with such a proposal, for, if the principle were adopted, he might find himself in a contest placed on a footing of equality with men who are respected for store of intelligence rather than cash; and that would never do, for if Toryism means one thing more than another it means the upholding of class privileges and class exclusiveness. Mr. PIERPOINT says it has been "calculated that to pay the whole of the members of the House of Commons would cost no less a sum than £240,000 a year." Bub surely hi serious in objecting to £240,000 as a for paying for 670 rulers, whou

£385,000 a year to the one person—to the QUEEN as chief ruler I It is a matter of course to say that the Tory candidate has no sympathy with the principle of "one man one vote," for that means that a vote in each case shall represent a man, and in so case represent property. There are working-men who have been led thoughtlessly to vote for Tory can- didates; but these are the days of universal their edu- cation, and it is time for electors to use thinking faculties, and ask themselves if it is ftnr that tha rich man, strong to begin with in illswing riches, should be made stronger by allo him half-a-dozen, or it may be a dozen, votes all as owner of property. It is a mockery of manll°°`lt and of every principle of justice, that property should in these cases give a qualification to vets- The poorest man that breathes should have the i right to protect himself by his vote in life ant, t' limb, and in the pursuit of happiness, an" e rich man should have the same right and no inert The workman who supports a candidate oppose" to the principle of "one man one vote" deserves to be oppressed by the Tories in the future as his forelathers were oppressed by them in the past. Let him be just to himself, and remem- ber that if the Tories could have had their waY he would not have been permitted oexercise the franchise at all. Lord SALisingair to even signed office rather than be party a narrow extension of the franchise to workinell in towns ; and, later on, he fought Mr. GLAnsr°;4ol tooth and nail, until Mr. GLADSTONE 1113Stehise him on the question of conferring the franc--ii, on workmen living in the country. The f°r"t t coming General Election is one of great Inmnsitzlit to the masses. The Liberal party are readY wci a programme of reforms which is calculate the improve the lot of every working-man 11%.03 kingdom. To go no further than the restors'io of the land to the people—that in itself will bans the effect of relieving the labour market in tnii'e and of adding to the wealth and happiness country. We We need to free the school, the cllll-0' and the land, to improve our licensing laws'ad shorten the hours of miners and railway-men': fe to remove the hundred and one abuses which 'fibe crept into the State. And how is all tlifori is te,e6 done? Not by sending selfish, stand-stdl to Parliament, but by returning earnest, WoAll°o hearted, go-ahead Liberals, who are these reforms reforms and will redeem their pledges'

Charles Holder, a Ship Canal labourer, was summoned ,o Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, to answer a 3harge of trespassing in pursuit of game, at Halton, on the 3rd inst. P.S. Costello and P.C. The Sergeant noticed that the defendant's pocket was rather bulky and an examination revealed a hare with teeth marks across its back. TED REMOVAL OF SNOW.

Mr. Heyes asked whether it was not possible to em- Loy a number of men with advantage in clearing snow l'off the footpaths, and in putting cinders or other rub- bish on the roads in certain places.—After some con- 'ersation the matter was left with th. 3 Health Corn- ittee to do the best they could.
DISEASE IN THE TOWN.

The Health Committee's minutes contained the report of the Medical Officer of Health for December, which stated that there had been,97 births and 44 deaths, being at the respective rates of 37.54 and 17.03. 12 deaths occurred amongst children under one year, and eight between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused "Iree deaths. There were 30 cases of infectious disease reported during the month, of which 12 were typhoid ifever and six scarlet fever. The medical officer added
liseasefia

'—l have visited and inspected most of the localities froi which cases of infectious disease were reported, and attribute many cases of typhoid and scarlet fever to deep ashpits with imperfect drainage. I am pleased tol report that the nuisance of sulphuretted hydrogen, escaping from the works in the township where Chanc Claus process is carried on, has during the month of December been reduced to a minimum as far as my observations are concerned, and I am glad to state that there have not been any complaints made to me. Thern were five patients in the Accident Hospital and nine in the Infectious Diseases Hospital. The Committee recommended that the salary of Miss Warburton be ad- vanced from £3O to £4O per -annum.—Mr. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes and spoke in high terms of Miss Warburton's capacity to the work she had to per- form.—Mr. Cook seconded.—Mr. Beech said he had a, strong objection to raising the sLI triei at the present time seeing that the termination of the Board was so' near at hand ; in fact if he had his own way he would 'go in for reducing some. He moved an amendment that the minute be not approved.—Mr. Wright said the matron's predecessor had £52, and Miss Warburton came in the understanding that her salary would he increased if her services were satisfactory, and she had won high opinions from the medical men, clergy, and others dur- ing the sixteen months she had been in charge of the hospitai.—She was in every way entitled to the money —The minutes was carried, only Mr. Beech, whose amendment was not seconded, voting against.

BREAKING THE NEWS TO THE QUEEN. The news of the Dukes death was broken to the Queen at Osborne as gently as possible, and it is satis- factory to know that the great shock her Majesty expe- rienced has not affected her health. The Queen is deeply stricken with grief at the loss of her favourite grandson, and she forwarded a sympathetic message to the Prince and Princess of Wales immediately after the fatal news 'arrived. TELEGRAM FROM THE PRINCE OF WALES. The Lord Mayor received the following telegram : .

"Our beloved *son passed away at 9- a.m.:—Alberti Edward." A copy of this was immediately affixed ont-I ide the Mansion-house, where a large crowd quick', collected and read the news with sad eagerness. Union Jack was at once hoisted at half-mast on _ Mansion-house, and the great bell of St. Paul's slowl3 tolled the intelligence to the city. The Royal Standard is flying at half-mast on the Tower of London, and many lublic buildings in London are honouring the mournful lent in the same manner. The Lord Mayor sent the following telegram to the IPA( ce of Wales :—" Profoundly moved by the sad news. Have communicated it to our fellow citizens. We ten- der deep and respectful sympathy with Royal Highness in this your great sorrow and national calamity." RECEIPT OF THE NEWS. The startling i. ews of the Duke's death was received in London as a great shock. It had been hoped all along at there was a ray of hope, but this has been dashed the ground, and the most profound sympathy is :pressed for the Royal Family and especially for the rincess May, for whom none but the tenderest condol- !noes are expressed. From all parts of the country come telegrams itating that the news of the Prince's death had created i profound impression. Sympathy with the bereaved family is universally expressed. The telegrams from the Continent and all parts of the 7orld show what a deep and painful impression has been by the news of the Duke of Clarence's death. LONDON IN MOURNING.
lld tt oh a 1 _ xpre.ssed Prince,— - r - al t r

The death of his Royal Highness Prince Albert Victor Christian Edward, Duke of Clarence and A.vonflalo, which occurred at Sandringham about nine o'clock on Thursday morn;ng, gives fresh startling, dramatic, and even appalling illustration of the truth of the saying that " it is the unex- pected that happens.' Only 28, and about to be married to a beautiful and charming bride! Had the Royal Duke's position been one of the humbl- est, instead of one of the most exalted in the land, such a setting of the sun of hope would have attracted general and sympathetic notice. But the heart of the Empire was concentrated upon the ar- ranged happy event. The day had been fixed, the bridesmaids selected, and a programme arranged which, to borrow the language of the Laureate, would have seen the exuberance of feeling "melt into stars for the land's desire." How tragically different, alas ! is the event which has happened. The joyful expectations of a few days ago have been dashed to the ground and shattered. The voice of congratulation and rejoicing has been quenched in mourning and woo. Desolation and anguish take the place of eager and happy anticipation,and instead of the merry wedding peal the nation will listen to a sad funeral knell. HIS LAST ILLNESS.

Yesterday London was in deep mourning, The shops in the West End, without exception, display mourning ,boards, while all bright coloured goods are removed from the windows.

THE COURT MOURNING, &c. The Press Association says that the Court mourning has been fixed by the Queen for six weeks, with three veeks public mourning, and three weeks' mourning for tie army and navy. , Dr. Laking remains at Sandringham, in attendance upon the Princess of Wales and the Princess Mary of 'reek, who are suffering from the effects of their severe filiction. ~ It is now regarded as .unlikely that Dr. Reid will per- mit the Queen to go to Sandringham. .. The Duke of Edinburgh is superintending the funeral arrangements in London. MEMOIR OF THE PRINCE. The Duke of Clarence and Avondale, whose untimely death the nation are now mourning, was born at Frog. more, on the eighth of January, 1864, but was so elicate a child that his baptism did not take place until tho 10th of March succeeding, when he received the name of Albert Victor Christian Edward, the Queen being present as Godmother. The birth of an heir to the throne in succession Le the Prince of Wales, was ,iled with delight by the whole empire, and many civil .d other rejoicings took place. The young Prince', arty education was entrusted to private tutors and pro. remora, under the direct control of the Prince of Wales, Id it was finished at Trinity College, Cambridge, and University of Heidelberg. Previous to his entering an undergraduate however, he passed two years as a eve} cadet on board the Britannia, joining in 1877 with is younger brother Prince George. In 1879, he was .ppointed a midshipman, and started with Prince George in a voyage round the world in the Bacchante. All the important British possessions were touched at, and everywhere the young princes were received with warm demonstrations of loyalty and affection, especially in ;the Australian ports. The tour lasted three years and fits events have been graphically recorded in a volume lited by their tutor, and written by the princes them- alves. Soon after his return, his Royal Highness went to the University, where he was a general favourite. On the termination of his studies ho proceeded to Aldershot to prepare for the army, and in 1885 he was transferred in the rank of captain to the 10th Hussars from the Royal Artillery. His Royal Highness, while with his regiment, took the ordinary routine duty with us brother officers, and was very popular with the °idlers. In the autumn of 1890, the Prince was with, .iis regiment the 10th Hussars, in garrison at York, where he was very popular net only with his - officers but with West Riding society general ri..quently --wok part in the meets connected • well-known packs of foxhoonciff- hunting Ai tl Riding. It would seem that after returning on Monday, the 3rd inst., from the funeral of Prince Victor of Holienlohe, the Duke of Clarence did not feel well, but with the de- termination of youth to shake off an illness which did not seem serious, he went out shooting on the Wednesday, and, it is feared, aggravated his indis- position. On -Thursday he seemed to be sufferinc from an ordinary cold,and remained in the house all day, but it was not thought that he had caught the malady,which by this time had made its unwelconit presence felt in the Royal household, and which was very prevalent in the locality. Invitations bad been issued for a dinner party at Sandringham House on Friday evening to celebrate the duke's 28th birthday, amongst the guests being the Duke and Duchess of Fife, the Duke and Duchess of Teck the Princess Mary, to whom lie was betrothed, and the Princes Adolphus, Francis, and Alexander of Teck. The Duke of Clarence, however, was unablc to ne present, being confined to his room, and on Saturday morningit was thought advisable to call in Dr. Laking, of Pall-mall, who, with Dr. bent, had hac'k been in attendance during the seriousl illness of Prince George, hi s brother. It was then clearly seen that the Duke was suffering from a ,severe attack of influenza, accompanied by pneu- monia. The doctors, however, were able to report favourably, and on Monday morning the public had some consolation in the statement that his Royal Highness's strength was well maintained. The duke's condition on Monday evening was so fully maintained that it was not deemed necessary to issue formal bulletins, although care was taken to inform the Queen, and a reply was sent to the Lord Mayor of London, that "the illness of the Duke of Clarence continues to pursue a somewhat severe course, but his Royal Highness's condition' and strength are favourable." But on Tuesday the Royal patient was worse,anc the Prince of Wales gave instructions that medical' bulletins should be issued twice a day and posted at Marlborough-house. The doctors were almost in constant attendance. and Sister Victoria, who so skilfully nursed Prince George. was installed in the sick room at Sandringham, the Princess of Wales, however, devotedly taking a mother's share in the nursing of her son. The first bulletin issued on Tuesday was— Sandringham, Norfolk, Jan. 12, 10.30 am, With regard to the illne.zs of H.R.H. the Duke of Clarence, the inflammation of the lungs is pursuing its course, and the strength is well maintained, but no improvement can yet be reported in his Royali Highness.

The Prince and Princess of Wales, Prince George of Wales, the Princesses Victoria and Maud, the Princess Mary Victoria of Teck (the Duke's fiancee) and the Duke and Duchess of Teck, were all at 'Sandringham at the time of the death. The Princess of Wales, bore up with great forti- tude until all was over, and then completely broke down. The Princess May, for whom the deepest sympathy was expressed, was prostrate with grief. Messages of condolence arrived during the day from all parts of the world. The "British Medical Journal " gives the collowint particulars of the Duke of Clarence's illness :—His Royal Highness was first attacked by influenza on January 7th, but first felt really ill on the Bth, when he was unable to attend a birthday dinner given in his honour. ln the 9th a patch of pneumsnia consolidation was dis- Avered at the base of the left lung. On the next day dul- ness on persussion and tubular breathing were present, and the temperature was 1034, pulse about 90, of good character, and respiration 30. The intellect was per- fectly clear. No material change took place till the 11th, when, though the base cleared up considerably, the right middle lobe became implicated. On the 12th nourishment was taken well, and the pulse continued good, but in the evening the patient became more exited, and during the night delirious. Delirium con- tinued and cJnstituted the &mil:fent features of the ill- 'nets in its latest phase.

div.head: BURGLARY AT TDB BIG FIELD.
div.p: BURGLARY AT TDB BIG FIELD.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. John Brundrit, Joseph Frederick Burke, a middle-aged man was charged with having on the 11th inst. bur- glariously entered a hut on the Ship Canal works at Big' Field and stolen a pair of trowsers and a purse contain- ing 305., belonging to Charles Sibley, a navvy. On the,' night in question Mrs. Sibley, who was ill in bed] wakened her husband and said there was a man in the room. He, however, considered she was dreaming or nervous through illness, and took no need. Next morn-1 ing he found that his trousers had been taken from the foot of the bed, and also the purse and money. P.C. Royle and a watchman named Samuel Hill deposed to I seeing the prisoner loiter about the place, and the formerl said when he apprehended him at Warrington on Tues-1 day he had 12s. in his possession and was wearing a new pair of shoes. The prisoner was remanded for a week,l for the attendance of Mrs. Sibley who states that shel identify the intruder in the bedroom. AGED PERSONS' TREATS AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. The annual treat to the aged people of Runcorn las been fixed for the 27th inst. The first treat to the aged poor of Widnes will take place on Thurs- day next.

The Runcorn Board of Commissioners at their last, meeting had a great variety of subjects before them, and the report of their proceedings is very interest- ing reading. The most important matters dealt with were the proposed VeLicular Bridge across the Mersey, and the endeavour to induce the Ship Canal Company to construct deep docks at Runcorn. With regard to the former,there is no doubt that the Bridge would be not only an incalculable boon to the twin ,towns of Runcorn and Widnes now so far divided, but also to a very much wider area on both the Lan- ,!ashire and Cheshire side. Under these circum- stances the Commissioners are acting wisely in en- listing the sympathy and support of the surround- ing local authorities, because, and there is no use disguising the fact, the County Councils will need some pressue to ihduce them to adopt the scheme of Sir Douglas Fox or any other, al- though the estimated cost of £150,000 may not represent much on the combined rateable value. Skilful and powerful advocacy on the part of the local authorities on both Councils may have great weight, and the promoters of the scheme may rely tupon having the aid of Alderman Muspratt and Mr. Thomas Snape, hand Mr. P. Speakman and Major Liasle h urst.

As to the Deep Docks this is, as Mr. Lightburni observed, a question of such supreme importance' that the ratepayers will be glad to see that, al- though it was introduced in an election address, it is not being allowed to drop into oblivion like so many election cries, which, having served their purpose at the polling booth, are carefully put aside to be resuscitated when another appeal to the " free and independent" is made. There will be little satisfaction to the Runcorn people in tht Ship Canal, if all the large ships that venture upon its depths are to majestically sail past the port. There ale many vessels laden with " Manchester goods," which will find Runcorn Bridge, high as it is, an impossible barrier and if Runcorn has no accommodation for them, they will have to dis- charge at Liverpool as now. A deep dock or even a commodious "lay by" might induce them to come up to the ancient port, and save the heavy dues of the seaport city,in addition, very probably, a saving of time, which to business men is a saving of money. It might also also be shown that a deep dock at Runcorn would be an advantage to the Ship Canal Company by providing traffic for their Bridgewater undertaking, but the deputation when they gain the interview may be trusted to thrust all points home. May they succeed in their object ! , 8:

The Press Assodiation states that Cardinal Manning died at 8.20 on Thursday mcrning. Death was due to bronchitis, symptoms of which first appeared on Thurs- day week. His Eminence grew weaker on Wednesday night, and began to sink in the early hpurs of Thursday morning. Losing. consciousness at 7.30, he never ral- lied. The Cardinal's secretary informs the Press Asso- ciation that he passed away calmly. The late Cardinal, who succeeded Cardinal Wiseman, was the son of Mr. William Manning, M.P., a London merchant, and was born at Torreridge, Herts, in 1808. life joined the Romish Church in 1851, and was created cardinal priest in 1875. His Eminence was well-known for his theological discourses, and he took. great interest n the working classes 'by whom he,,..,s held in the highest esteem. lil. Mr. Edward Whitley, p,l-7,-for the Everton division if Liverpool, died on Thu'rsday forenoon. Mr. Whitley was born in 1825 add did not marry till 1872. He was partner in the legal. firm of Whitley and Co., of Liverpool, and was maycc of the city in 1868. He sat for the borough as a Conseryative from 1880 till 1885, and subsequently for the Everton division, The news of the death of itir: Whitley caused much ;urprise, as well as regret, in Warrington where ho was )retty well known' being a nephew of Sir Gilbert Green- dl and brother of the vicar of Daresbury, and having poken at public meetings of Conservatives in the town. lie firm of Messrs.'Grefenalt, Whitley', and Co. own ex- nisive breweries at St. Helens too,and the death of Mr. Vhitley, M.P., Wag a Sicrblovkiii the officials and ser- rants of the firm. The intelligence was received at 12-50 in the form of a telegram from the firm's offices at Liver- pool, which stated" Sorry to say Mr. Whitley died this moruing at ten o'clock." No intimation of the serious illness of so popular a member of the firm had been re- ,eived, and no one was prepared for the sad news. :lough the late Mr. Whitley had no active participation in the management of the Bt. Helens Brewery, he was extremely popular in the bilitrict. He and his father were the original solicitots to the old St. Helens and Runcorn Gap Railway Company, one of the earliest rail- way undertakings in the kingdom.

Elizabeth Robinson, 16 years of age, daughter of a chemical labourer,residing in Back James-st.:died at Widnes Accident Hospital, on Wednesday night, from severe burns received on Monday. The girl was lying on the hearthrug, when a piece of burn- ing coal rolled from the fire and set her dollies in flames, which were extinguished by P.C. Cochrane. Her injuries were so serious that there was no hope from the first. -Mr. W. T. Husband, the de- puty coroner, held the inquest yesterday afternoon. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death "; Aid complimented the praiseworthy efforts of the :onstable to save the girl's life.

Church- street, by the school children. The following characters were represented, viz. : Peter Patter, alias Don Quixote; Willie Wastle, alias Sancho Panza ; Handy Andy, after- wards a captain in the army ; Tom Tug, afterwards a lieutenant in the navy; Dolly Dimple and Willie Wimple, the babes in the wood; Rattan' Rovin' Robin, a plough- man on the farm Hoojiken, and a general favourite of the Lady of the I:ea, owner of the estate; Lucy, Peggy, and Biddv, the Lady of the Lea's domestics; Dame Dur- den, of Hoojiken Farm ; John, Dick, Joe, Jack, and Humphrey, labouring men at the farm; Melly, Betty, Dolly. Katey, and DorothY, serving girls at the farm, soldiers, Handy Andy's comrades; and sailors, Tom Tugs shipmates. The beautiful costumes were made by several ladies ol the parish, and the stage appliances and ,scenic effects and properties bore ample testimony to 1 the thoroughness of the Rev. S. C. Barmby's training. The music, full of spirit and vivacity, was ably rendered on the pianoforte by Miss Thomas, of Hemp-Gill. BEFORE THE MA.GISTR.I.TES. CHARGE OF PREPARING A BAD SREEP FOR SALE. At the Warrington police court on Monday, Jos. Shaw, butcher,Bredge-st., was charged by Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, with having in his possession on the 6th inst., at his slaughter-house, in Bank-street, the carcase - of a sheep which he had prepared tor sale but which was unfit for the food of man. Mr. P. Davies, defended. —lnspectorPowell deposed to finding the sheep hanging with some beef on the defendant's premises, and to at- tempting to take it away, upon which the defendant, who then came in,said he should not do that as he did not want his name in the papers, and struggled with him to prevent him taking it. The defendant said it should not 5,,0 until Mr. Norman had seen it. Witness tried to find him but could not, and then had the carcase removed to the Town Hall.—By Mr. Davies: The carcase was dressed as if prepared for food, but he could not say it was so pre- pared—Dr. Gornall, Medical Officer, deposed to finding the carcase to be that of an ill-nurtured sheep. He certified it as unfit for human food. He never saw the internal organs. He could not say what disease it died of. There would be most likely some congestion of the lungs.—lnspector Norman gave corroborative evi- dence, and said he cut its kidney open and it was rotten. The animal was not a lamb, or it was a very old one.— Mr. Davies said the defendant had some 33 sheep in Arpley cricket field, and as the snow came on and covered up the herbage the sheep got over the fence into the bowling ground to get access to some plants, the sheep in question being hurt in doing so, and found dead in the snow. It was taken to the slaughter-house and flayed and was going to be taken away in a trap to be used for food for Mr. Shaw's pies and dogs, but a hail- storm coming on prevented this being done. The fat had all been taken off, and there was not a skewer in it, and nothing to suggest that it was being prepared for sale. The carcase mortified and was to be given to his pigs and dogs.—John Melia, constable at Arpley, corro- borated as to the sheep dying in the field, and said the defendant's man brought it away to be skinned. There was no snow on the bowling green that day. There was boar frost.—John Cartwright, the defendant's assistant, gave evidence and denied that the sheep or lamb, as he called it, was prepared for sale. It was 251bs. weight, the weight of a well-developed lamb. The fat had all been taken out and put in tubs.—Inspector Powell re- called said there was one skewer in the carcase.—The Chairman said the Bench considered the past conduct of Mr. Shaw above suspicion, and they were sorry for him in his present position, but they believed there was not the slightest intention to sell the abet for human food, though he had acted very foolishly, and must be more careful in future. The case was dismissed. CRUELTY TO CHILDREN.—THE STATE OF PIEEPOINT-ST. HOUSES. At the Borough Police Court, yesterday morning, Moses Williams, forgernan, 116, Pierpoint-st., and Eliza Williams, his wife, were charged with cruelly neglecting their children, on the Ist inst. Mr. B. Shearer, prose- cuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians. He said he visited the house on the date mentioned, and found one of the children running about barefooted. A younger child was suffering frosn disease of the eyes. and it seemed to be neglected. All the children were in a very filthy condition, the stench being horrible. There was not an ankle of furniture in the kitchen, and there was nofire, and all the panes in the windows were broken. The male defeadant earned 355. a week, and he was , very attentive to work.—Detective-Sergeant Monoghan said he found the children in a filthy condition. a The mother is a very drunken wovnan, and had been .!„ previously prosecuted. —lnspector Spinks said he visited -, the house several times in September last. The children were then in a filthy state and seemed to be neglected. On two occasions the woman was lying drunk in the house. When he called the male defendant was always at his work. They were convicted in September of keeping a house of ill-fame. The female defendant called several witnesses, who said they lived in Pierpoint-street, and denied that there had been any neglect of her children. —Alderman Harrison, who presided, said it was a very disgraceful case, and the female defendant would have to go to jail for two months. The male defendant was also responsible for the conduct of his wife. If he was more of a man he would see that his children were better cared for. If he was brought up again on a like charge he would not be dismissed, but in the present case he would be dismissed.—Dr. Gornall remarked that there were some other cases of a similar kind in Pierpoint- street. Some houses in that street were a disgrace to the town, and the Sanitary Committee had a hard job to keep it in shipshape. He thought that landlords ought to be held responsible for the state of their houses, and if he had anything to do with it he would prosecute them and deal with them severely.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRTNGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. &TlM:WT.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), Messrs. R. Garnett, L. Voisey, and John Geddes. THREATS AT A LODGING HOllSN.—Daniel Grant, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with using malicious threats towards Mr. Brouchemite, the proprietor of the model-lodging-house, Friars'-greea.—lt appeared from the evidence of prosecutor and others, that the prisoner visited the lodging-house late on Thursday night, and went into a room occupied by a man named Regan. Be attempted to to take a waistcoat which, he thought, contained money. He then commenced to strike the man about the face,and caused him to shout "Murder." The deputy of the lodging-house came and ejected him from the room, and Mr. Brouchemite ordered him to leave the house. He returned the next morning, and "had some words with Mr. Brouchemite, and,accord- ing to the evidence, threw a basin at him, wheroupon Mr. Brouchemite struck him with a stick in self-defence Be then pulled out some sharp instrument, and threatened to stab the proprietor in the ribs with it.— Prisoner, said that he returned to the lodging-house for 4d. which was due to him, presumably on account of being turned out of the house. Mr. Brouchemite refused to give it to him, and commenced to strike him with a StiCk.—Fle was ordered to find two sureties of £lO to keep the peace for six months, or in default one months imprisonment. jogN WARRINGTON."—The well-known youth, John warrington, was charged with having been found on the premises of the London and North-:Western Railway Com- pany, at Bank Quay, at twenty minutes to tenon Friday night, for an unlawful purpose.—A police-constable said that at 9.15 on the night named he saw prisoner going lute the high level sidings. As he did not come back, he went in search of him, and found him in a second-class carriage in the sicling.—A representative of the company staid that they suffered considerably during the winter months from this sort of thing.' People frequently cut the straps and took them away, and did other damage. —John was discharged on condition that he went to the workhouse. This he promised to do. MoNDAy.—Before Aldermen Francpmb (chairman), Sutton, and Harrison. Dix.—Richard Lewis, drunk in Sankey-street, on Saturday night. He was fined 35. DReN AND DISORDE WlX.—James Lynch was charged 'with being drunk and disorderly in Stanley-street, on Saturday night, and with assaulting George and Margt. Wheeler and Bridget Turner. Be was sent to prison for a mouth's hard labour.—George Houghton, drunk and disorderly at Market Gate, and assaulting P.C. Chrimes and damaging his coat, at a quarter to one on Sunday xnorning. P.C.'s Bolton and Chrimes said the prisoner

was drunk and disorderly,and would not go away. They took him into custody, upon which he lay down and kicked and got hold of Chrimes in a very dangerous sort of way, and would not loose his hold, and damaged his coat. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs.—Alice Daley, Mary Scully, and Alice Healey, were summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Edward-st., on New Year's Day. A warrant was ordered for Daley, who did not appear. They had been very violent, one of them being armed with a poker. All three had their faces smeared with blood. The defendants present denied the charge, and said they were attacked by a man because they remonstrated with him for assaulting a boy whose face was "smothered in blood." They had previously been several times convicted of being drunk and disor- derly, but were now fined the costs only, 3s. 6d. each.— John Cokeley, drunk and disorderley, in Tilley-street, on the Ist inst., was fined ss. OBSTRUCTION.—RaIph Norman, Lomax's Yard, Hall- street, charged with obstructing Horsernarket-street, by allowing a handcart to stand unnecessarily long, on the 4th inst., was dismissed with a caution. Doos UNMUZZLED.—Councillor Francis Dixon, of No. 1, Arpley-street, was charged with having his dog at large unmuzzled. The defendant pleaded that the dog was blind, and was with him, and could not go three yards from him, being blind. P.S. Chantler who proved the case said the dog rushed at every horse and cart that passed.—The defendant denied this, and said the dog was almost completely blind.—William Price, 4, Pier- point-street, and John Potter, 118, Bewsey-road, were charged with similar offences, and they and Councillor Dixon, were fined 3s. 6d. each.—Mr. Dixon on paying his fine expressed his indignation at the proceedings and said it was of no use talking about cruelty to animals, as this enforcement of muzzling was nothing else.— Alderman Harrison said he agreed with him, but it was the law and the Bench were compelled to carry it out. Councillor Dixon, with much warmth, said the Act did not say you were to take a dog that was blind. Alder- man Harrison was supposed to know something about animals.—The Chairman said it was not the dogs eyes but its teeth that the Act was concerned with.—Coun- cillor Dixon repeated that it was cruelty to animals, and the law did not say you were to punish animals to give protection.—Mx. Dixon then, with much anger expressed on his countenance, quitted the court. PLAYING AT BUNG IN TUN ST/MT.—Joseph Whitlow, son of Joseph Whitlow, 20, Fennell-st., James Glover, son of Patrick Glover, 3, School Brow, and James Bull, son of Henry Bull, 7, Brick-st., all boys, were charged with playing at a game, which they called "hung," in Brick-st., and let off with a caution and payment of costs. CHIMNEY ON FlE.—Edward Mains, 43, Oliver-st., for having his chimney on fire on New Year's Day, had to pay is. TUESDAT.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. J. Guest.

A DESNIZTER.—Thomas Mulligan, a young man, was charged with being a deserter from the Argyle regiment, stationed at Stirling. He had presented himself at Orford Barracks for enlistment, and on being charged with being a deserter he confessed.—He was remanded to await an escort.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr,John_Fairclough (chairman)
and Mr. E. M. Crosfield,

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Edwards, of Dial Court, 24th appearance, was charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous night in that Court. —P.C. Clough deposed to the circumstances.—The defendant denied the charge, and said he was anroyed by some youths coming to his door and window and shouting "Come out Edwards," and he came out to drive them away, when the constable took him into custody, and in bringing him to the station tore the coat off his back. The Chairman cautioned the defendant as to his making such statements about a constable, and expressed his disbelief in them, and in his denial of his guilt.—He was fined ss. and costs.
TI HIIRSDAT .—Before Captain Ridgway (chairman), and

.. „ Mr. James Fairclough. CHARGE or WIPE DESERTION.—Idatthew Flannaghan, tanner, of Orford-road, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guardians, with leaving his wife and two children chargeable to the Union. on October 31st. The case was adjourned till the 28th of January. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman), and

Wright and Dr. Gornall, MARRIAGE V. APPRENTICESHIP.— Mary Preston, 33, Watkin-st., fustian cutter, was summoned by William Tiddler with absenting herself on December 21st, from his service, she being his apprentice, putting him to the loss of Bs. 6d. The defendant's plea was that she had got married. Alderman Harrison pointed out that her marriage did not release her from her obligation as ap- prentice, but asked the prosecutor if it would not almost pay him as well to release her.—He said he was willing to buy her off.—An order was made for her to return to work and pay the costs at 6d. a week the defendant foregoing his claim to the Bs. 6d. CRIIIILTY TO Hoasss.—Henry Finney, hawker and horse dealer, was charged with ill-treating a horse on the 11th January at Latchford.—lnspector Dowty, 11.5.F.GA.., proved the case. He said on the date in question he saw several gipsy's vans in Poacher's-lane, off Thelwall lane, Latchford, and in a field near two horses belonging to the defendant. There was snow in tne field, and there was no sign of food or shelter for them. They were suffering from exposure to cold.—He had only summoned him for one horse.—Mr. Hill, veterinary surgeon, and a police constable corrobo- rated.—The defendant said he fed the horses well, and at night put a cloth round them. He could not get shelter for them —lnspector Dowty said the defendant could have got shelter if he had liked.—He was fined 20s. including costs.—George Finney, of no settled abode, whose wife appeared for him, was charged with committing a similar offence on the same date.—lnspector Dowty said the defendant had horses in the same field which were being treated in the same way as the other animals. He had found the two Finney's at Newton on Thursday, subjecting horses to similar treatment. These men were not men who could plead poverty. He had seen them at a fair with a hundred horses.—Alderman Harrison : Don't you think starving them in that way would depreciate their value.—The Inspector replied that the value of onel of their horses ruled about £2.—Mr. Hill corroborated. The defendant's wife volubly denied the charge.—The defendant was fined 20s. including costs.—John Doug- lass, of no settled abode, was similarly charged as to illtreating a horse on the same date and on the same spot.—The horse was suffering from wounds and covered with lice, besides suffering from being exposed like the other animals in the field without food or shel- ter. Mr. Hill corroborated. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs.

div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Gaskell, inn., and Mr. J. Brock.

A ROGUE AND A VAGABOND.—Edward McCormick, 88, Midwood-street, was charged with being a rogue and a vagabond, and behavior, in an indecent manner. The offence complained of was committed on Saturday night, and three women were called who identified the prisoner P.C. Almond apprehended prisoner. He pleaded not guilty, but the bench sent prisoner to gaol for one month with hard labour.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. Idoxnay.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds, and Mr. A. Thomas. A WartNixo.—Henry Jones and Thomas Pownall, youths, were summoned for sliding on the footpath in Church-st., to the danger of passengers.—Superintendent Large said the case had been brought as a warning and the defendants were discharged on promising to pay the costs. DISORDERLY Coxnucr.—Harriett Baxter and Richard Bostock were charged with behaving in an indecent manner in Brook-st.—flostock was fined 20s. and costs and the woman who had been 17 times convicted was sentenced to one month's hard labour.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches plikyed on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. WIDNES v. RUNCORN.

The above teams met on Saturday, on the Lower- house-lane ground. before about three thousand specta- tors. Brennan kicked off for Widnes, who pressed at once, but Runcorn relieved, and a neat kick by Barber returned. Houghton, however, returned the ball again well into the home quarter. A nice even game was wit- nessed for some time, neither side being able to gain ground. A smart kick by Houghton made the game look dangerous for the home team, but the ball was brought back and some exciting play followed near the visitors' line- The ball was once more in midfield, and Davies received a pass and made a fine run down the field, but was neatly stopped from placing the ball over. The leather was brought out once more, and Houghton got hold and made an attempt at goal, but failed. Even play followed, and when half time was called neither side had scored. The second half opened in favour of the home team, and in a few minutes the ball was dribbled down near the Runcorn line, but was returned, and play centred in midfield once more. The Widnesians seemed to have the best of it for some time. Runcorn now worked up the field, but the homesters returned again, and the ball was kicked in touch several time in the home quarter. Being free again, it was taken up the field, and some neat passing was witnessed amongst the Runcorn men. Hollings- , worth eventually got hold and placed well over, but the kick at goal was futile. The visitors still had the best of the game, and it looked as if they would score again, add when the whistle sounded the Runcorn were deolared victrionus by one try to nil. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, _ JAN U NOTES ON GAMES AND 1 WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ATHLETICS,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, _ JAN U NOTES ON GAMES AND 1 WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. ATHLETICS,

Football fixtures were sadly interfered with on Sabi-- day by the frost and snow. Many grounds were in ;oo dangerous a condition to admit of plav, and many of the Rugby clubs in Lancashire were obliged to postpcne their engagements. The Leeds club failed to put in an appearance at the Warrington ground, although dm local executive had gone to considerable expense in ht,v- ing the ground cleared of the snow. The turf wasin capital condition, and thoroughly fit to play onr and tm conduct of the Leads club was severely commented upon.

Berry, the county and international half back, often makes his presence felt in club football, and he had a large share in the easy conquest of West Leigh by their neighbours at Tyldesley. The trial of strength between Widnes and Runcorn was of a vastly different descrip- tion, as the latter had their work cut out to win by a try to nothing. Walkden appear to be dead out of form, and they had to accept another reverse at Birkenhead, where the Wanderers won their West Lancashire Lelgue fixture by nine points to four.

Last season:Somersetshire could turn out a formidable fifteen, but they are now much weaker, and in beating them on Saturday by three goals and two tries to a goal and a try Yorkshire only did what was expected from them. The changes that had been made in the forward ranks of the winners told a tale.and this department was decidedly strengthened. Nichol!, the Brighouse Ranger, was in great form. The Yorkshire backs all came off with credit, but they were never severely tested.

Associaticn players are more fortunate than their Rugby brethren. It is not often that their fixtures are upset by stress of whether. Still several were cancelled on Saturday, but nene of these were of first importance. The five League fixtures that were down for decision were brought off satisfactorily, and there were some , startling results. We an getting accustomed to strange exhibitions by the Darwen players, and whatever they do no longer esUlSee a cry of artunieliatoot. Their corn plate helplessness against a really first-class club is pro- verbial. They have been ruthlessly dealt with in many of their League encounters, but came in for the heaviest punishment at Burnley. Despite the great activity of M'Owen, their undersized but skilful goalkeeper. Darwen were actually beaten by nine goals to none. This has only once been equalled this season, and that was when Notts County were similarly successful against Accring- ton. On such form as this Darwen can scarcely hope to retain their membership in the League.

A genuine surprise was the victory of Everton at Nott- ingham. Notts County had hitherto managed to escape defeat in the presence of their own supporters, but they new had their colours lowered by three goals to one, all of which were secured after the change of ends. Oswald's position as centre forward was entrusted to Walkerdine, and Williamson, a local youth of promise, was tried on the right. Everton were much the cleverer team and won by soperior football. This was especially noticeable in close quarters.

It was of course taken for granted that the North End would win their return with West Bromwich Albion, even allowing for the enforced absence of Drummond. But as matters turned out Preston could only put an a goal to nothing, the forward play being anything but satisfactory. They found themselves opposed to a stub- born defence, the goalkeeping of Reader being particu- larly sound. Beckton, of the reserve, filled the gap created by Drummond's suspension and shaped fairly well. There is some talk of Dewhurst getting himself into condition again, in view of the importance of the League championship and ths F.A. Cup ties.

Accrington are very hopeful of escaping from the dreaded last four. They have conquered Aston Villa and Stoke within a week, and are now only a point be- hind Notts County. They would have beaten Stoke even more decisively than by three to none had it not been for the very fine defence of Rowley, Clare, and Underwood. Aston Villa lost the services of Brown, one of their half backs, owing t) an accident, and yet they were six goals better than Derby County. Both these Midland clubs have failed to fulfill the promise of the early stages of the season.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse,on Wednesday morning. Idr.Bal- harry presided,and there were also present the Rev, G. nearly i?rozen to death,—Mr. Heaton said he had a lot of female. wood-cutters employed at his place.and they did not want fires but worked hard and are able to keep them- selves warm. .--S3TRORG. Mr. HOOD.WRIGHT asked if the Board of Guardisaae

CoTla-CIO-t-Mything towards putting down the iniquitous system that prevailed in the fisatian cutting trade of giving people RI for binding their children to fustian cutters. The system, he thought, was an iniquitous one, and white slavery was nothing to it. Oxt of LS cases of applications for school fees 40 were of fustian cutters. The thing wanted looking into somehow or other.—Mr. Hitharox said they coifed not stop the system. —Mr. Reicraera thought the abolition of the system, would be a beneficial thing for this Union.—Mr. Don- SON: We cannot stop the law.—Mi. Hoon-Wunian- We can do such a thing as have the law altered.—Mr. Diaotat said they could express their opinion and let it go forth to the world.—Mr. Gmr, said the new factory act absolutely prohibited the employment at fustian cutting, among some other trade's, of girls under VI years of age.—Mr. Jour Houcurrots: That is a very good law.—Mr. °wax said he felt they ought to assist Mr. Hood-Wright in his object as far as they possibly could.—Mr. W. Houourox said thee had had ttott

_ subject before them in relief Committee and he had al— ways condemned that re-binding system. He suggested that the Clerk might make a representation to the next Poor-law Conference, and perhaps prepare a paper on it. It would be of great benefit to that Union to ventilate thelquestion.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said that almost nine relief cases out of 10 were of persons connected with fustian cutting, and that re-binding system was, he believed; the cause of it all.—Mr. &few said if there was a law that

young women could not be employed at fustian cutting till they were 18 years of age he was sorry for the laws Be believed that befor• they were 18 girls were quite capable of attending to various duties and thus bring in a return to their hardworking parents. Mr. Shaw also commented upon what he understood were methods of payment in certain fustian cutting shops. If there were any suggestions to be made he suggested that they be sent direct to the masters.—Mr. Hoot' WRIGHT approved of tho idea of bringing the matters before the Poor-law Conference ; it really wanted bringing before the Labour Commission. Children were taken and for the sum that was paid they were apprenticed to a business in which they oeuld never get a decent living and the streets were filled with prostitution.—Mr. HEATON said he did not know where some of the Guardians had got their opinions of fustian cutters front. Ile had had something to do with fustian cutting and he had very great plea- sure in knowing a lot of fustian cutters, and he might say they were equal to any other class, at Cockhedge or any other place. Fustian cutters conducted themselves as well as most people. He did not think it was the manufacturers that were to blame. They found fustian cutters with good dwellings, and earning from 12s. to 14s. (Cries of "when ?" and" where ?") He had looked at the wage sheets of one of the largest places in the town, and he saw that six men in one room never got less than 19s. Plenty of women in that place got 143. (" Oh oh," and "No, no.") They were all paid by the piece, and if a man had a mind to be idle he only got 2s.—Mr. How" Winona, said he know na.. thing about fustian cutting, but he knew it was a bad system that required propping up by giving women £1 on appreaticing. At McCorquodale's and other decent businesses the parents were not given £l.—Mr. Ilneyon said a master fustian cutter summoned people repeatedly before the magistrates, and if there was anything seri- ously wrong the magistrates would not convict. -Mr. HOOD WRIGHT : But it is the law.—Mr. Owina•said that when profits of 200 or 400 per cent were got the law . wanted altering.—Mr. HOOD WRIGHT : It is worse than slavery.—Mr. DIGGLE alluded to a case in which a woman because of an advance of 153. for Walking ..

Day, from her employer, engaged herself for nine months, and during that time the master got half her earnings. With regard to the wages mentioned by Mr. Heaton there had been times when they were got, but wages fluctuated and they did not get half that now.—Theaunx pointed out with regard to the suggestion that the matter should be brought before the Poor-law Conference, that the Conference had no power to legislate. That was a question that should be dealt with by some such body asthe Labour Commission. He thought it would be well if a girl before following any employment should have an opportunity of being taught domestic work and domestic economy and have &certificate to show that she had attained a proper standard before she was permitted to be a full timer. (Hear. hear.)—ln answer to a question the CLI4IIIC said bethought the proper thing to do was fer the fustian cut- ters to bring the matter before the Labour Commission. —Mr. HEATON said the fustian cutters had a trades union, and they knew whether the statements that had been made were correct. The sovereign that was paid was a binding to bring the parties within the law, and if the parents took it that Board could not helpit.—Mr. DIOGLI They do it through poverty.—The discussion then dropped, and the meeting terminated. 0

div.head: THEY SANG ON THE SHIP'S DECK.
div.p: THEY SANG ON THE SHIP'S DECK.
" Home, home. sweet sweet home • Be it ever so humble there's no place like home."

Blessed be the memory of John Howard Payne for writing this song. Who doesn't know it? Who hasn't sung it ? Full of hnpa, full of heartbreak, its melody has girdled the globe. In July, 1891, a large party of Cornish people sat on the deck of the good ship City of Paris, bound from New York to Liverpool. They were coming on a visit home after long absence. And as the ship ploughed the calm waters,they sang" Home,Svreet Home." But a gale came on, and for two days most of them had other matters to occupy their attention ;they were too seasick to sing. Then the Welsh coast was in sight, and they sang once more louder than ever. And so it goes on everywhere—illness and trouble spoil the

music. "My wife never knew what it was to be well." Thus writes a husband, and here's the rest of his letter. "She always felt tired and languid," he says," and never got enough rest. She had a dreadful bad taste in the mouth, with a sinking, gnawing feeling at her chest, and her food seemed to do her no good. She had also a dry hacking cough which people'said was a Churshyard Corgh.' She went as thin as a shadow and had to alter her clothes and make them smaller. Now better and now worse, she went on suffering like this for ten years, and took all kinds of medicines, cod liver oil among the rest. She saw several doctors who sounded her chest and asked if any of her relatives had died of consump- tion, leaving the impression on her mind that she was consumptive herself. Now, as her mother had died of consumption, she felt sure she was going into a decline. Thiee years ago I was much concerned about her. She had sick headache all the time, pain in the sides and I legs, and used often to faint, and got so weak I had to take her in my arms and lift her in and out of bed. People asked what was the matter with her, but she could scarcely describe her condit ion, for it was an all gone feeling, making her fit to drop down. Even going upstairs would exhaust her and make her feel faint. In November, 1888, a book was left at the house, in which my wife read of a case exactly like hers, and she exclaimed "That is just my complaint, and as it been cured by Mother Seigel's Syrup, perhaps my ailment is I not consumption after all." "I got the Syrup and she found relief from the first bottle, and soon grew quite strong. The backing cough left her and she now enjoys her food. I consider that a bottle of Seigel's Syrup is worth more than a week at the sea-ride. Before taking this medicine my wife's life was a misery to her. You are at liberty to publish this statement if youdesire to do so." '(Signed) J. Jay Smith; Compositor, 25, Sudely-Street, Islington, London. This is another instance of indigestion and dyspepsia being mistaken for consumption. Fortunately the little book referred to, revealed the error in time to enable Mrs. Smith to treat herself for her real disease a,nd, bring about a quick recovery. But cases with a less happy ending constantly occur. We would again im- press the fact upon the public that consumption, rheu- matism, gout, bronchitis, kidney complaint, and nearly all affections of the throat, lungs, and nerves are vir- tually symptoms of indigestion and dyspepsia, for the reason that they are caused by a poison in the blood directly resulting from a torpid state of the stomach' liver, and bowels. Therefore however strongly the indications seems to point towards one of those so-called diseases, your true course is to take Seigel's Syrup,which removes the radical difficulty which lies at the bottom of nearly all physical suffering, viz., indigestion, and dys- pepsia. Who has not sometimes said, "Oh, I have such a head- ache—l can scarcely see ?" What makes the head ache? Well, the disordered nerves, of course. And what throws the nerves out of order? Let us see. "For fifteen years," says Mr. W. D. Evans, of Brynawel, Mount Pleasant, Swansea, "I had been a great sufferer from indigestion and flatulency. I bad a bad taste in the mouth, with pain and distress after eat- ing, and my bowels became much swollen. I felt lan- guid and out of spirits, and had great pain across the temples, which at times was so severe I could scarcely see. I saw several doctors who were unable to give me more than temporary relief. In December, 1890, I told a friend of mine, Mr. W. Lloyd, Rising Sun Hotel, Morriton, how bad I was, and ho advised me to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. After taking two bottles all the pain and oppression left me, and I never felt so well in my life as I have dOne since. I eat my meals with relish, and feel light and comfortable afterwards. This remedy has worked a miracle on me. It is a blessing to man-
kind." Headaches proceed from indigestion and dyspepsia. Use Seigel's Syrup and your head will sit on your shoulders like a flower on its stalk.

div.head: YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN; ASSOCIATION,
div.p: THE YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN; ASSOCIATION,

The annual meeting of the Warrington Young Men's Christian Association was held in the room of the Association on Tuesday evening. Mr. John Fairclough J. F., presided. The secretary's report which was read, has already been published, but it was stated that a piano, which was much needed by the association,had been presented by Mrs. Parr. Mr. R. E. Garnett, the treasurer, read his report, which showed that on the general account there was a debit to the association of about ..£19., the vear having been started with a balance of sa on the wrong side. Three of the trustees had promised to clear off half the debt. With regard to the f arriisbing account, there was a balance in hand of SR A great deal of the expense of the past year would not arise every year, such things as papering and preparing the rooms having had to be attended to during the past twelve months. Mr. J. Hough- ton moved the adoption of the reports. Mr. J. Critchley seconded, and the motion was carried. The following officers were appointed fot the forth- coming year :—President, Mr. J. Charlton Parr ; vice-presidents, all, with the exception of the Rev. W. Graham; who has left town, were re-elected; furnishing treasurer, Mr. R. E. Garnett. The elec- tion of general treasurer was left to the committee. The election of the committee was next proceeded with, two scrutineers, Messrs. Tanner and Ogden, being appointed. The following consti- tute the committee :—Messrs. J. T. Pattison, Dutton, W. Bayley, A. R. Horden, W. Wyllie, J Critchley, Shaw-Green, C. 11. Kerry, T. Wallington, S. B. Stringer, J. Houghton, J. S. Garland, sen., B. Crowder, A. Horrocks, J. Toft, W. 11. Butler. A , new rule was passed forthe benefit of those who joined the association during the course of the year, which provided that such members should pay 4d. if they were under 17, and those over that age should pay 6d.. for each month they were members of the association. A vote of thanks was passed to the secretary and treasurers, to the chairman, also to the late secretary, Mr. T. Wallington, and to the honorary auditors, Messrs. J. Critchley and S. P. Jones. The meeting concluded with the singing of the Doxology.
