div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held': at the Dutton Union on Tuesday afternoon. There- were present Meosrs. Mclntyre (in the chair),Bagu-- ley,. Weir, Aaron, Heywood, Pickering, Baxter,. Lewis, Bretherton, Parr,W hitiow,Brandreth, Speak, man, Lea, Bate, and Taylor,the Heir. J. W. N. Tanner, and Mr. J. Ashton, clerk.

ME. /MAKER'S CLAIM 071 t TEE BOARD. Mr. Baxter said in accordance with the understanding at last meeting he had seen Mr. Linaker as to his claim, on the Board for remuneration for extra services in con— nection, with his temporary clerkship. He went with the object of making some amicable arrangement, but did not succeed so well as he expected. The Board had offered him £lO, and he asked for £3O, and he (Mr. Baxter) suggested to him that they should split the difference, and that he should accept £20,, but he would not admit that that would adequately " pay for the extra work he had performed. After his- explanation to him he was inclined to look more favourably on his claim than when' he voted against paying him £3O. It had not been made clear to him. before that the £lO offered him actually came out of the late clerk's and the present clerk's salary,. as he' understood it had. Some of the Guardians had been under the impression that it would be paying him twice over,,whereas the amount had only been paid once. He-. very much doubted whether if the matter went to arbitration the Board would not have as much to ,pay as Mr. Licaker claimed. Mr. Linaker did intimate to him that if Mr. Stokes's motion had been carried he should not have proceeded further with the matter. Mr.. Baxter, pursuant to notice, proposed that the resolution of the Board deciding to offer Mr. Linaker £lO be rescinded, and that the Board propose arbitra— tion on the claim.—Mr. Speakman seconded.—Mr. Aaron proposed, an amendment that £2O be offered. He was dead against arbitration, and if Mr. Linaker did not accept £2O he must take the matter to court, and he (Mr. Aaron) if he did so would be pre- pared to carry the case to a higher court to defeat hint. —A lengthy discussion raised by Mr. Edwards, took place as to whether the amendment was in order.—The Clerk ruled that it was.—Mr. Taylor seconded it, remark- ing that the Board had been under the mis-impression that the £.lO was in addition to what they had paid the late clerk, and that therefore if they paid Mr. Linaker £2O they would be no worse off than before.—Mr. Edwards maintained, despite the Clerk's ruling,,that the amendment was out of order. What was-the use of it, he asked, if Mr. Linaker would not accept £2l/ ?—The Chairman : I must rule you out of order.—Mr. Edwards : We are making a lot of children of the Board.—Mr. Weir: I have been here a good few years, and never heard of arbitration before. I think we are still a lot of school boys.---Mr. Baxter expressed his readiness to accept the. amendment.—lt was then put, and 15 voted for it, including Mr. Bax- ter himself.—Mr. Aaron subsequently to put the matter in order proposed as a substantive motion, the rescind- ment of the Board's previous decision as to the claim, and that the sum of £2O be offered to him.—Mr. Parr : 'propose that the sum remain as it was, £lO. (Laugh- ter.)—The substantive motion on being put was voted for by-12 Guantiand,B: only voting against,and was therefore declared carried. SALARIES OF SCHOOL ATTHEDANCE AND ENCitTIRY

OFFICERS. • Mr. Taylor proposed that the enquiry officers at Run- corn be, in accordance with a recommendation of a meeting of the Runcorn Guardians, dispensed with, ex- cept Mr. Bowyer, and that his salary be as heretofore,£s a year.—Mr. Speakman seconded, and the motion was carried.—A motism was proposed by Mr. Aaron, and se- conded by Mr. Heywood, for increases of the salaries of the other officers who act as school attendance and en- quiry officers, but the motion was lost. AN INSURANCE DIFFICULTY. Mr. Aaron complained that a widow who had been in receipt of relief from the Board, since the death in May last of her husband, who had paid into a certain insur- ance society, between 30 and 4.0. years, received only £8 10s. from the societ,y, instead of £l5 which she ought to have had, but which they declined to pay because of her having misrepresented his age, and no certificate of his birth being obtainable. After some conversation on the matter, the Chairman advised Mr. Aaron to bring the matter up another time. lan. EDWARDS'S REFUSAL TO SIGN FOR A reams:. Mr. Edwards said at the last meeting a letter was read as to his refusal to sign.a rate, from his co-overseer for Frodsham, Mr. Davies. Ile had done so because he wished all thomonies derived from the rates should be paid into the bank, in the joint names of MI% Davies and . himself, lie asked the Board to recommend to Mr. , Jones, the assistant overseer, that this be done. If they did this, he would sign the rate, bet he objected to public money being in the hands of one man.—The Chairman told Mr. Edwards that he hild his and would have the Board's full sympathy, but it was not a matter ' for the Board to deal with. There was no further business.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WAR RINGTON,

After the revelation at the meeting of the Town Council, last week, I don't see how the Corporation of Warrington can escape the responsibility of deal- ing with the insanitary area which has been defined and reported upon by the Medical Officer of Health. Dr. Gornall's report is clear and emphatic, and the only question that remains is how best to grapple with an obvious difficulty. It will rever do for an Inspector from the Local Government Board to have to come down and lecture us for glaring sins of omission ; nor will it do to suggest that the area is as good as the people who dwell therein. Two blacks have not yet begun to make one white. Besides an unsanitary area may mean an epidemic extending to the classic residences of even Coun- cillors and Aldermen. It is startling to learn, on the authority of the Chairman of the Sanitary Com- mittee that the death rate for the borough for the past year, will be nearly 25 in the:thousand.

A Conservative Ward meeting is not, as a rule, a very lively "function," but, notwithstanding that the brand-new candidate has been industriously perambulating—in spite of sciatica and other ad- verse influences the meetings held this week are about the imliveliest on record. From the time when the meetings were supposed to begin until the votes of thanks were being proposed, a few listeners dropped in, at not very frequent intervals, and in a casual sort of way. They did not seem to expect much, and they were never disappointed. lir. R. Pierpoint at one of the meetings blamed the Liberal Unionists—he took it for granted that there are some in Warrington—for the negative manner in which they were supporting their principles, but the Liberal Unionist, when 'he is caught, might easily retort that everything is negative about Mr. Pierpoint. His programme is certainly a blank negative, for his whole time is taken up, not in showing why something should be done, but in giving reasons why everything that anybody proposes, should not be done. A modern man--even a Liberal Unionist—can hardly be expected to sup- port a negative in a positive way.

I hear that Mr. Ribert Pierpoint was tripped up rather unexpectedly at his meeting in Latchford Ward, on Wednesday evening. Be caid that whilst the Gladstomans had been vapouring about Free Education Lord Salisbury had given it, whereupon an elector asked how it was that he still had to pay for his children's schooling? This was a poser.which 3dr. Pinpoint sought to evade by saying he "really could not enter into details." But in this case the "details " are everything. If education is "free," why is there anything to pay? It would seem that the" vapouring was on the part of Tory candid- ate; and it was seen-to be vapouring when be was unable to back hiS statements by a plain answer to a plain question. If he can profit by experience, he will " sing small " for the future about " Free Education.

It has often been whispered that Sir Gilbert Greenall had a secret wish to be " elevated " to the peerage, so as to be of equal standing with a noble lord who also has a share in the tied " pubs" of Warrington. Seeing, however, that this Parliament is near its close, when Sir Gilbert will become poli- tically extinct, there is only a poor chance of this "elevation "ever taking place in the orthodox way. This would be unfortunatkif there wcre no other way of gratifying Sir Gilbert. But there is another way,and Mr. John Roberts, in that eminently prac- tical style of his, has fo,und it. He never speaks ot Sir Gilbert except as his " noble friend," and if you look at it this will settle the whole thing. If everybody decide to call a man " noble " why then he is a noble. The only difference between the peer and the peasant is in the estimation of the people among whom they live, and if everybody will adopt Mr. John Roberts's style Sir Gilbert is as good as "elevated."

The government departmente in London always take a decent time to consideti a proposal that is laid before them, but the Local Government Board has given an extra amount of consideration to the application of the Warrington Corporation to bor- row £5,000 for the baths extension. Perhaps the holidays came in the way,and it would be unreason- able to expect the superior officials to let a little provincial item of this kind interfere with their festive meditations. But, lam glad to see that the reply has come at last, and, as it is favourable, that the new baths will be built, This reply will give relief to some people, and especially to Alderman Francomb. He will not now be called upon, accord- ing to promise, to bear the cost of the premature foundation-stone laying, and, above all, it will not now be necessary to hide under a bushel, or some- where else, the pretty little trowel that was pre- sented to him.

Old soldiers are not often eloquent. Shakespere's old campaigner. Othello, on addressing the senate, Ands himself less an adept at the utterance of words in their august presence than he is at the perform- ance of deeds in the tented field, and tells them;— Rude am I in my speech, And little bless'd with the soft phrase of peace.

Sergeant-Major Hardy, of Warrington, however, is an exception to the rule of which Othello fur- nished an example. He is an old Crimean soldier, who proved himself a man of deeds in the memor- able campaign; but at the aged tr en's dinner last week he showed himself equally proficient in point of words, and made a sder oh of thanks to the Com- mittee, which was really excellent, and was ad- mired by all who heard it. Sergeant-Major Hardy, can give some stirring accounts of his experiences in the Crimean War, though he never obtrudes these upon those be meets with. He is, I may men- tion, a writer as well as a speaker. In 1886 he proved his literary ability by obtaining the prize of 21 guineas offered by " Tit Bits" for the best article descriptive of the contributor's career as a soldier. Warrington ought to be proud of having such a man in its midst, and' I hope he will live long enough to participate in many more of the annual aged men's dinners, and that a place will always be found for him there, though the old men like the old women should become too numerous to be accommodated.

A stranger sojourning in Warrington for a short time and observing the character of the play bills exhibited about the town might be disposed to cre- dit the Warringtonians, I fancy, with a most ab- normal appetite for the "blood and thunder " element, in theatricals. As I think of the pictorial presentments of scenes from different dramas per- formed in Warrington during the past eight weeks or so, my blood almost curdles, such a catalogue of horrors does my mind pass in review. I will in- dicate a few of the pictures that I have seen in the course of the time I have mentioned. A man lying pn the ground having just been despatched by an as- sassin ;"another man taking a shotlat the slayer with a revolver. A man throwing another down a preci- pice. A murdered girl lying on a bed and a woman demanding of a man by whom the deed has been done. A fashionable young lady, gaily dressed for some festive scene, in the flush of beauty and ani- mal spirits, and a man about to strike a dagger in- to her bosom,and hissing the word " Revenge" into er ear. A young lady lying dead on the iloor,hav- ing just been shot by the revolver of a fierce assas- sin, standing over her.

--- Then, quite recently there was to be seen a bill representing scenes in another piece, these being -represented in four squares, three of them being murder .scenes. In the first a knife was being die- covered in a tree—suggestive of murder In the second a man was failing, probably having been thrown, over a waterfall, and another man below was making sure of his destruction by discharging a revolver at him as he fell. In another square a man was being hurled overboard from a steamer, and while one passenger was leaping over to res- cue him, another was taking a shot at him with a revolver, as in the other picture, t. o make certain. The latest piece of sanutnary n alism of tliis kind is n a pictorial exhih.tion this week of some scenes in aplay being performed here, one of which is a man lying bound fast, across the railway line, and a locomotive passenger engine corning close upon him. What is the meaning of all this ? It is the demand that creates the supply, and it is clear that in Warrington as elsewhere, the more death there is in a play that is, violent death, the more life there is in it to the mind of the aver- age play-goer. "Shakespeare spells ruin:" moaned an experienced theatre proprietor in London years ago; and murder too evidently spells success in Thespian orthography.

FARMERS AND HIGIIWAY AUTHORITIES. Sir,—l notice in your last issue a letter by " Nemo " complaining of the neglect of the roads about Grappen- hal As that village is as strange to rge as Timbuctoo, I can't gainsay any of his remarks about the state of the roads there ; most likely they as as bad as what he has described. But as a small farmer living within the dis- trict of the Warrington Highway Board, I must say this much that my experience and candid opinion is that however lenient the Board may be with farmers in the Grappenhall district, they are too often found interest, ing themselves with farmers' private rights as to how high a certain hedge must be, Sze. As an illustration. I have but to cite my own case. The other day I received orders from the Board to cut a certain hedge adjacent to the highway, though the hedge in ' question had beers kept straight and in no way inconveniencing the foot- path. " Nemo" assumes there are men "kept on the road who are paid for doing the needful." And so they are, but "the needful" seems with a good many of the em- ployes of the Highway Board to take the form of how to pass the day by gossiping to passers-by and giving false or exaggerated reports of matters to their masters.—l am yours Sec.,

SHOP ASSISTANTS' HALF HOLIDAY MOVE- MENT. Sir.—As a constant reader of your paper, will you kindly allow me a little space in it. to set forth a few ' comments, on the half-day holiday movement, which is I just now being brought to the front by the shop assis- tants of Warrington. I feel sure we shall have your sympathy and help in this matter, as your name during the time you were in Blackburn, and the time you have been in Warrington, has always stood identified with any good measure or work which has been for the ele- vation, or for the benefit of the working classes. Let us ' take, for instance, the factory hands of this country. Their employers are bound down by a certain code of by- laws limiting them to so many hours of labour, and not to go beyond that limit. Legislation' steps in and says, "so many hours shalt thou labour ;" but not so with us. The employers in our case are at liberty to frame and make their own by-laws as far as regards the hours we have to make during the week. Legislation does not interfere on our behalf. As a body of shop assistants, I think we are only fighting for our rights in this matter, Considering the many hours we have to make from Monday morning to Saturday night, are we not entitled to a few hours recreation in the week ? Is there no one with some little influencein the town that will take upon themselves to help us in this matter ? If Hine is, and our object is gained, we shall have reason to thank them for the help they may render us in this cause. We look upon the Sabbath as a day of remotion for the soul, ' but can we be blamed for using it at times as a day of recreation for the body, when it is the only day that we Ive a few hours to call our own? It is very hard for us to be deprived of this privilege, when such towns as , Earlestown, Widnes, and St. Helens, so near to our own can have their Thursday afternoons to themselves. I have made inquiries from the shopkeepers of the different places, where this half-day holiday has been in force for some time now,as to whether they have suffered in business, or whether it has made any difference or not ' in the amount of money they took previous to this tak- L ing place and since, and I have had a satisfactory reply from each one of them. I elicited from the chairman at most o the meetings that were held at Widnes during the agitation of this movement that it was the shop- k s themselves that took the matter in hand there and cirried it to a successful issue, feeling that they stc )d in need of a rest as well as their employes. I am afraid we shall have to wait a long time, if it has to be left to the shopkeepers of our own town. What -
RUSTIC.

want to do is to bring this matter before the public in order to enlist their sympathy ; if we can only do this our cause will be carried. May I suggest to those assistants that are under the nostrum of coercion, who dare not lift up their voice on this matter, that they can take up a pen and s:3t, forth their grievance in the public press, which '3 free to all. It is a case of "now or never "with us. Do not let it be left to just a few to fight this battle of freedom and justice, but let each one work as if it depended on himself alone. If we can only do this, vic- tory will be ours in the end.—Yours truly, T. B. D. 103, Manchester-road. EARLESTOWN PUBLIC HALL ONCE MORE !

Sir,—" We may be happy yet ; "for, if the old adage iscorrect that " When Rogues fall out, honest men come by their own," then, similarly when a clique of Commissioners come to open disagreement, there is a chance for those who have suffered througu cliquedom, to have more attention paid to their just demands. I felt quite cheered when I read, in your columns, the report of the last Commissioners' meeting. I felt that, at last, an ugly combinatien was broken up, and that, at any rate, there would be a chance of our innumerable and just requests being forced upon their attention by those who had rebelled against wasterul expenditure ! Metaphori- cally I clap Messrs. Ratcliffe and Mac Mahon on the back, and say" Go it again! Give it to 'em hot !" Am I too hasty in supposing that the former of the two rebels will follow up his saving policy, and demand that the outrageous extra expenditure proposed on the Public Hall shall not be carried out ? Can I expect him to fight the point, when his property will be so much improved by the addition of that (to be) three- cornered outrage on common sense ? I fear not—he is only" very human," and will probably say,—as the fellow does in the Pantomime—" when you touches my pocket you touches my feelings !"

As for Mr. Macmahon, I suppose he will subside again 1 into the old jog trot way of saying " ditto," to all that the two—l beg pardon,—one leader (Mr. Ormand) may say; though I could wish there was as much fight in or wrong—as there is in his countrynaan,Tim

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUA

working-men having votes. John Ruskin says—" A bad law is one that cannot hold, however much you or- j dain and pronounce it." Read Carlyle with all your I heart, and with the best attention you can give,and you will learn from him the eternity ot good law, and the need of obedience to it. Take heed, ye who oppose our just voting power! For justice demands a change in such a bad law. Dr. Houston tells us that all men ought to have equal voting power—" One man one vote." 01 no, say those who can live and revel among the beauties of nature simply because their purses are bigger, to often by op- pression, spoiling of widows' houses, and other ill- gotten gains. They can have a dozen or more votes, while we poor working-men, who create their wealth, build their gorgeous halls, furnish them with all that is within them, and even make and wash all their clothes, are to be thankful to be allowed the privilege to help them to dress themselves ; make, and mend and clean their boots and shoes, for which they trample us under their feet,and tells we are very foolish and wicked because we point out when, and where we are hurt !

_ . But take heart, fellow workers, Dr. Houston has pro- mised to give us the benefit of skill ; and do all he can to cure the above ills, and a number of others which I will tell you about next time I write you. Let us try and help him to be successful, Come lade come ; rally for the fight! Down with wrong, and atraggle for the right Yours truly, A WORKINGMAN ON GUARD. -- SCIENCE AND SENIIMENT; MIXED.

"The fact is, that at the present moment there is not a shadow of trustworthy evidence that abiogenesis does take place, nor has taken place, within the period during which the existence of life on the globe is recorded,"—Huxley " Anatomy of Invertebrates" (1177) p. 39. Sir,—Asa professed evolutionist, " I must own to the soft impeachment" of entertaining an unbiassed belief ir abiogenesis. This is merely a betief—a sentiment opinion—without actual basis of fact. This prospective hypothesis—the beginning of life without previous life— or spontaneous generation—has not a single fact to se, port it ;so at present, as far as human knowledge goes, It Is non-existent. Now, as I am Int arrogant enough, to think that my opinion upon this philosophic fancy would be any value to your readers,l declined—and stil- decline—to vvastetime and effort upon such barren dis- putation. If Mr. Butler wishes to abiogenesize the readers of the "Examiner" he must select a more " for- , midable opponent than Mr. Peers." I should thus, from I an active participant, become an amused spectator of I the docking of a cockscomb.

div.p: Healey' I have tried to find out how a contract, ostensibly placed at £5,000, and advertised as su.ch, should be sprung to £7,7oo—the ratepayers not having been con- sulted. I have tried to discover the straightforwardness of asking for designs for a building to cost £5,000, and then giving the contract to a firm who completely ignores the amount stated, goes in for something more expensive, and gets theaward ; and it may be, whilst some of the other competitors knew nothing of the in- creased cost that the rate raising division, Commis- sioners had quietly made up their minds to go in for. Where is the fairplay here ? And I have tried to find out how our Surveyor is going to fill his new offices, if the present offices are too small for one man and a boy r Are the Commissioners going to supply each of them with a bedroom, that when overwhelmed and exhausted with their arduous duties, they can retire for some much needed repose ? But, Sir, questions without end could be asked in con- nection with this hair-brained scheme of the new public- hall ; and though it appears to be of no use asking the perpetrators of this huge folly for their reasons: yet they may take it from me, that the " Local Government Board" will be asked, and they will assuredly rant to know why the rates of an important parish should be played "Ducks and Drakes" with, at the instigation of a Clique, whose interests and instincts are widely at variance with those of the long- suffering parishioners. I have puzzled myself also to know how it is there is so much " Ormand " in the monthly reports? Wouldn't it be well, for variation's sake, to have a little more—say---" Thompson," and a little less " Ormand ?" The latte: is certainly troubled m:th the Cacoethes loquendi to an alarming extent; but we know him so thoroughly now, that it would be quite a relief to hear some other orator " on the joh."—Yours truly, Newton, January 14, 1892
CLIQUE HATER.

EARLESTOWN PUBLIC HALL. Sir,—No doubt your excellent report of the preceedings of the Newton Commissioners at their last meeting would be highly interesting to your readers. That portion of it headed" Cookery and Laundry Work : Who is to pay for teaching ?" was, to my mind, so amusing- that the temptation to read it twice was irresistible. The resolu- . the subject, to my surprise, was mimed by Mr. Jpson, and seconded by Mr. Forster. It is apparent from this, that Mr. Thompson Intends to abandon the role of " silent member." Evidently he has actually resolved to make an attempt to perform his duties se a Commissioner. Mr. Forster-,-Totc-has awakened to the fact that in a very few months he will have to give•an account of his stewardship. Up to the last meeting he had made no very brilliant -bid for popularity, but, fear- ing to meet the electors with so empty a book, he male a desperate rush to fill a few pages. However, my special object in writing tins letter le to trumpet the achievements of Messrs. T h9mpsoi Forster, but to call the attention of your readers . inconsistency of Mr. Ratcliffe. At the previous meeting, in his most eloquent language, he supported the pro- position of Mr. Emmett to spend an additional sum of 1 £2,700 on a Public Hall, under a subterfuge which I am cons :need is transparent to every ader of the Examiner." Such an expenditure is merely a reckless squandeling of the ratepayers' money, supported by a very small minority of owners of 'property contiguous to the site of the proposed Public Hall, Mr. Ratcliffe him-- self being one of the largest. Mr. Ratcliffe's position must be painful to himself, for it is very humiliating to fall so low in the eyes of the ratepayers after deservedly enjoying their highest esteem for so long a time. The severe criticism his conduct has received has evidently roused him to a sense of his position, and he makes a frantic attempt to regain his former popularity, by pos- ing as a grc at economist in objecting to the expenditure of a paltry £25, which is all the ratepayers are required to contribute, in order that their daughters may be in- structed in those domestic accomplishments which they will find so necessary in the future, namely, cooking and laundry work. It would almost appear that there had been a split in the camp of the el'que, and that the good old times had returned when there was no Blue Bottle element to pull the strings, and the Commission- ers wei.at liberty to speak their minds conscientiously, unprejudiced by any prior arrangemer Notwithstand- ing the strenuous exertions of Mr.. Ratcliffe, it is not a little singular that no amendment was proposed, from which it may be taken that the discussion upon the expenditure et' this trivial amount was greedily seized upon by the objectors as a means of airing their eloquence, and diverting attentim from their attitude on the Public Hall question. It was a palpable attempt to draw the red herring over the trail, but Mr. Ratcliffe may rely upon it, that the actions in voting away nearly £a,ooo ; proposing Mr. Thompson as a Commissioner, and voting to supply the Railway Company with gas at 2d. per 1,000 feet less than the great body of ratepayers will not be easily forgotten. Neither will the series of speeches I made by him at the last meeting tend to restore him to the position he once held in the opinion of the rate- payers. Yours, &c., CRITIC. January 12th, 1892. P.B.—Before closing this letter I should like to ask, through your columns, if the overseers had been con- sulted as to the finding of the money for the Town Flail ; also what sum will have to be found annually for g as, coal, attendance repairs, additions, Sze. Perhaps Mr. Ratcliffe will oblige by giving this information. THE REPRESENTATION OF WARRINGTON— WORD TO WORKING-MEN. Sir,—The other night I went to listen to the address of Dr. Houston, as a Trades Unionist and a temper- ance man, and came away much instructed, enlightened, and completely satisfied that in him working-men have a clear-headed, a kind-hearted, and an able friend to fight for us. We Union men cannot hope to have from among those who move in ranks of the rich and cultured, a gentleman with a sounder judgment, a firmer grasp, and wider acquaintance with any just requirements than is possessed by Dr. Houston. His language was easy to be understood by us as Working-men,; close, and to the point. There is a Latin proverb which says" The face is the index of the mind." Thought is the force which moulds. and makes not only the human face but the vast uni- verse, contended a divine to whom I had the pleasure of listening in one of our local churches a fortnight since. If so, then we have in Dr. Houston ono of the highest land be.L.type of men whose word will prove his bond;. land therefore we working-men may rest assured that, should we support him in every lawful way in our power, and at the same time, to do justice to ourselve3, we are bound to return Dr. Houston as our representative at the next General Election. I have been a householder over 21 years, a loyal sub- ject, a sober working-man, therefore had to pay my share of taxes, Sm., but have never yet been allowed to record a single vote at any Parliamentary election. Why not? you inquire ; simply because I hrve mostly lived, where I love most to live, among the beauties and swer,t-: ne of nature rather than amidst the din and smoke and :tench o" the town. Such a crime on the part of many thousands of working-men as well as myself has sub- jected a host of us to the same loss of voting posses and injustice. There is one thing the "judicious reader " of Mr. Butler's letter will have noticed. That is—the ease and completeness with which he disguises his great know- ledge of logic, and conceals his mature judgment. So efficiently and so naturally is this done that a careless reader would be apt to pass over the ground all unsus- picious of the hidden treasures beneath his feet. Like some other treasures they have to be dug for. Lei, us dig. Netehow he talks of Herbert Spencer's philosophy " being broken in two "unless abiogenesis is conceded as a fact of past time—while this philosophic fancy is to be argued upon as "the foundation of evolution !" I have been in the habit of regarding evolution as being based on facts well ascertained and generally acknow- ledged. This accords with Herbert Spencer's finding. But a new light has arisen. Has then evolution two foundations ; a Spencerian and a Butterian basis ? In- stead of being the basis of this hypothesis, I am inclined to regard abiogenesis as the crown—the as yet, undis- covered and uncertified pinnacle of evolution. hen I say I have no data for a newspaper discussion ch a subject, he most needs affirm that deficiency in subject—that the "subject was lacking in sufficient data." In the hands of the authorities he so pompously parades, it is, as a philosophical thesis,a proper subject for discussion. To impose this as a mere wrangle of unfruitful verbiage upon your readers would be an impertinence, in which I decline to be a party. Mr. Butler objects to two words I used—orthodoxy and practical. In deference to his wishes I withdraw the word orthodoxy in favour of Methodoroy. If he will champion the cause of Methodoxy in the question of man's origin lam ready and willing. Methodoxy is a good word, if it is rather mixed, philologically. In this respect it is all the more applicable to our critic, whose metaphors and methods are alike mixed. In him incom- patibilities are reconciled; the lion of evolution lies down with the lamb of Adamic exhortation. I have heard Mr. Butler discourse very eloquently in favour of evolu- tion. Probably this was before he received the hint from his spiritual superiors that such sentiments were unacceptable? Hence his natural and emphatic, No ! to my proposal. In my last letter I offered to discuss with Mr. Butler a subject of great iwportanco to all your readers. It would be a debate having a practical application to the religi- ous, moral, and intellectual condition of OUT people. Property discussed, with earnestness, honesty of purpose and moderation, it would not be a mere beating of the wind or an excuse for the venting of vituperative ver- bosity. Broadly and briefly stated:thus :—What7we know and t we are tad of the origin and early history of man be likened to a wedge, i.e.—a figure thick at one end tapering to a thin edge at the other. Now Vie 3tion is, which end first? Mr. Butler, as a local acher, is bound to present the thick end as being the representation of man's first appearance on earth. den and abrupt advent as a perfect man. Science that the thin end is the most consonant with the facts. Here we have a definite and a fruitful subject for discussion. If Mr. Butler is not under reumenical inter- dict on this point and will step into the arena, I will en- Mer, deavour to prove that lam not averse to discussion. Let e your correspondent shake off the fetters of intellectual bondage, follow the dictates of his conscience and reason to their logical consequences, and fear neither Pope, Cardinal, nor Conference. One touch of English soil Turn gives freedom to the slave ; would that this were so in- iSE3 T tellectually as well as physically! All the hums bl M inhuman, factors of the inquisition are with . e aso126 wanting only the potentiality for evil. Let us hope th corpse long disuse may destroy the propensity, as ratior in for a good has destroyed the power. We have evolution to tha read idDicksho for this,, among other blessings.—l am &c., seri a et, JOHN PEERS. kr 3 an Penketh,. 19, 1,1892. EXFCUTION OF THE GREENNOCK

MURDERER. Frederick Thomas Storey, late circus manag.r, was I executed at Greenock on Monday morning for murder- ing Elizabeth Stewart, a circus performer, by, stabbing •her, because she rejected his attentions. In the solemn procession to the scaffold he appeared the coolest of the party, and repeated the Lord's Prayer in loud, clear tones. A drop was allowed of 61t. 61n., and death was instantaneous. fief I THE LION HOTEL ENTRY INTO SHIP YARD. The alterations by Messrs. P. Walker and Son, the new proprietors of the Lion Hotel,. to ' building, which were recently sanctioned by magistrates, and included the formation of vaults and the making of an entry into Ship- yard, have been in progress far some days. The wife of Mr. Pickavance, leather merchant is the owner of the adjoining premises,a, workshop, in Ship-yard tenanted by Mr. W. Poole, glazier. She gave notice previous to the alterations that she would object to any encroachment upon her land. On Monday morning it was found that the builders were breaking through the wall of the hotel into Ship-yard. Thereupon Mrs. Pickavance em- ployed two men to look after her interests, and an animated dispute took place between these men, and Messrs. Walker's men, but no absolute violence occurred. A fence it may be men- tioned. had been erected close to the wall by Mrs. Pickavance, in assertion of her right, and this had not been interfered with ; not -was any attempt made to destroy it. During the altercation,the Town Clerk, Mr. J. Lyon Whitttle, made his appearance, and asserted that the yard was the property of the Corporation, and complained that &number of tiles in it had been removed. After discussion of matters, building was suspended until a, settlement was come to between the parties. Mrs. Pickavance, for whom Mr. A. Browne is acting, asks a certain sum from Messrs. Walker on condition that she is allowed the same rights in the yard as the other tenants, and that if the workshop is pulled down the firm will build her other premees. •;

Each cbild was also supplied with a bun or a penny. ACCIDENT' TO A RAILWAY PORTER.

On Wednesday morning, on the arrival of what ter known as the paper train from London at Bank Quay Station, Warrington, about ten o'clock, a par-- , cel porter, named Joseph Hill, in the course of his duties, opened the door of the front van. As he did so and entered the an some luggage fell, and a two,inctr gas pipe struck him, and owing to the weight of the luggage falling upon the pipe Hill received a painful injury,and was rendered partially. unconacioue. Mr. Ash urst„the station moister, and a medical gentleman who IMppened to be on the platform, picked the young man up, and Miser every care Wae paid to him, had hits:,:conveyed home. It is feared that Hill has sustained some internal injury.

Theßev. J. W. \Carley' gave an interesting lecture at the opening meeting of the second session of the Wycliffe Young People's Society on Monday evening The lecturer, who has been for a great number of years- in South Africa, and who took part in the Zulii,war, described the manner and modes of liv- ingpf the Kalfirs, Hottentot's and Boers in a most graphic manner, mentioning that so far as they had opportunities they proved themselves, net so ignor- ant a people as we in England seemed to think. He also,mentioned that the white people had taken with them their spirit bottle, and, as a result. the natives by their taking and liking of its contents were year by year fast diminishing in number,, Spedting of their religion, Mr. Varley said the greeter &ember of,the Kelm believed in and worshipped 'spirits, they having no idea of any God, which made it very difficult work for the missionaries sent there. But he was glad to say that their work was progressing, especially amongst the Basuto's, and he believed, in time, all the Kaffir race would acknowledge the Christian religion. At the conclusion of the lecture irote of thanks was accorded the. lecturer on the mot'on of Mr. S. Rowlands, seconded by Mr. J. ,Lowe, and supported ~by Mr. Borden, all of whom ?spoke in high favour of the way in :which the lee- tare had been given. Mr. Yonge who occupied the 'chair, referring to the lecture said it was encourag- ing to hear from one who had been able to see some of the results. of missionary enterprise, able to refute the insinuations of some writers in the press, that Christian missions were a failure. Mr. Varley responded:and the meeting closed in, the usual man- ner. BO4I:IhST.. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. le annual tea party In connection with Bold-at. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JANUARY 16, 1892.

In our national schools, both high and low, kind- ness, and our duty to animals, should form part of the curriculum, while every efort that science and investigation can command should be put forth to attain for such animals as aro needed for food, a Speedy, painless, and merciful end. As we have framed laws for the protection of domesticated and tame animals, so we should teach mercy—and where destruction is necessary—a painless mode ot death. And high time it is, that the machinery of the law be put in force to do away with the torture, Of wild animals, which under the name of "Sport," We daily immolate upon the a-tar of suffering, breeding and preserving them met ely for the grati- fication of the still lingering savage instinct in us, 'which delights in taking life. The idea will no doubt be unpopular and create resistance, and yet, he day must dawn when that savage instinct will become eradicated, and man will cease to seek and find pleasure in destroying our glorious animal life.

Yesterday, before Mr. W. Deacon, at the Widnes Police Court, Samuel Jones, fifty-four years of age, was charged with wilfully and maliciously setting fire to a stack of hay on Mount-pleasant Farm, Speke, the property of Miss Watt, of Speke Hall, doing damage to the amount of £2OO, between seven and eight o'clock on Thursday evening. Superintendent Keigt ley applied for a remand until Monday next. The application was granted. GAS FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Adrt. "WEDDING FESTIVITIEs." Richard Hackett, of 12, Tontine-at., St. Helens, driver for Mr. Whittemore, cab proprietor, was in charge of a wedding equipage attached to two horses at Earlestown, on Tuesday afternoon. On his return journey P.C. Wall found his horse wand- ering aimlessly about Chancery-lane, Parr, while Hackett was drunk. The affair caused some alarm in the neighbourhood, the horses being on the foot- path, and several shop windows narrowly escaped being broken. The officer put the helpless Jehu inside the carriage, mounted the box, and drove the driver to the Police Court, where he was fined next morning in the usual amount. J. & W. DUTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE 18 now on. Sankey-st.—Advt. Tin i PROPOSED EXHIBITION AT ST. HELENS. The sub-committee of the Corporation appointed to arrange the details of a fine-art exhibition, to be held in the rooms of the house in Victoria Park, have issued a report upon the subject. It has been decided to open the exhibition on the sth May, and it will remain open until the 30th August. Three rooms of the house are prepared for the exhibition, and space is provided for about 250 pictures. The librarian (Mr. A. Lancaster), who is officiating as the bon. sec. to the movement, has recommended that oil paintings and water-colour drawings should form the principal exhibits, with a few sketches in black and white and a small photographic col- lection. It is intended to have contributions from St. Helens and district before seeking loans from elsewhere. These will form the bulk of the first exhibition, but it is expected that in future years pictures will be received direct from artists, some of which might be purchased for a permanent col- lection. The Science and Art Department have promised to contribute a small collection of objects from the South Kensington Musenm. Applications will also be made to the council of the Royal Academy for a loan of one or more of the Chantry Bequest pictures, and to the Art Galleries of Bir- mingham, Monchester, Nottingham, Liverpool, and Sheffield for loans from their permanent collections. UPPER MERSEY COMMISSIONERS. Mr. Gessae,rre was re-appointed on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissim, his term of office having expired. BOWERS' BROOK. The Clerk reported as follows :—Messrs. Brown and Taylor, two of the members of the deputation appointed by the Local Government Board, had waited upon the United Alkali Co., Limited, on the 16th ult., with regard to Bowers' Brook. The deputation were informed that An arrangement had been come to between the United iAlkali Company and the London and North-Western --Away Co. for the latter company to enlarge the cul- ..rt •, and the United Alkali Co. agreed to at once clean ,ut that part of the brook which is in the neighbour- hood of Canal Passage. The United Alkali Co. also ex- pressed their willingness to enlarge the culvert through the Widnes Alkali Works as soon as the London and North-Western Railway Co. have carried out their en- largements. With the view of facilitating matters, Mr. Carey asked the deputation to instruct the Clerk to write to the London and North-Western Railway Co.'s engi- neer, urging him to give attention to the matter, and the Clerk had since been in communication with Mr. Footnew, of Crewe, who states that the matter has been referred to Mr. Stephenson, of Euston.—The report was idopted.
